abscesses and a course of metronidazole is the preferred treatment for

A 59 year-old man attends his general practitioner with a 10 day history
of watery diarrhoea. His stools are unformed, sometimes associated
with fresh red blood. He also has associated abdominal cramps for
which he has been taking paracetamol. He estimates a 5kg weight loss
during this period, and has struggled to tolerate food or fluids due to
significant pain on swallowing. He also has an intermittent sensation of
needing to defecate, but being unable to.
He has been diagnosed with HIV 8 years ago, and admits that he has not
been attending follow up, or taking his medications. He is unsure what
his last CD4 cell count was. He has had 5 episodes of pneumonia over
the last 12 months, the last one was 4 months ago.
On examination, he has dry mucous membranes with reduced skin
turgor. He has generalised abdominal tenderness, but no features of
peritonism, or organomegaly.
Observations
Respiratory rate- 18 breaths per minute
Heart rate- 110 beats per minute
Blood pressure- 104/60 mmHg
Temperature 37.7ºC
What is the most likely pathogen causing his symptoms?
Cryptosporidiosis
Clostridium difficile
Giardia
E Coli 0157
Cytomegalovirus colitis
Question 90 of 287
A 59 year-old man attends his general practitioner with a 10 day history
of watery diarrhoea. His stools are unformed, sometimes associated
with fresh red blood. He also has associated abdominal cramps for
which he has been taking paracetamol. He estimates a 5kg weight loss
during this period, and has struggled to tolerate food or fluids due to
significant pain on swallowing. He also has an intermittent sensation of
needing to defecate, but being unable to.
He has been diagnosed with HIV 8 years ago, and admits that he has not
been attending follow up, or taking his medications. He is unsure what
his last CD4 cell count was. He has had 5 episodes of pneumonia over
the last 12 months, the last one was 4 months ago.
On examination, he has dry mucous membranes with reduced skin
turgor. He has generalised abdominal tenderness, but no features of
peritonism, or organomegaly.
Observations
Respiratory rate- 18 breaths per minute
Heart rate- 110 beats per minute
Blood pressure- 104/60 mmHg
Temperature 37.7ºC
What is the most likely pathogen causing his symptoms?
explanation:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis is usually seen in patients who are
immunocompromised. It is a member of the herpes virus, for which
around 50-80% of the general population are seropositive. The virus lays
dormant until the patient is sufficiently immunocompromised.
Approximately 30% of all patients with AIDS will develop a
gastrointestinal CMV infection. This usually occurs when the CD4+
counts drop to below 100 mm3.
CMV can affect the gastrointestinal tract from the oesophagus to the
rectum, and symptoms depend on the site of infection. CMV
oesophagitis causes odynophagia and retrosternal chest pain. CMV
enterocolitis commonly presents with diarrhoea, fever, weight loss and
per rectal bleeding. Tenesmus can occur if there is rectal involvement.
Cryptosporidiosis is a protozoal infection caused by cryptosporidium
parvum. Immunocompromised individuals are particularly susceptible.
The incubation period is between 2-10 days (average 7) and symptoms
usually last about 1 to 2 weeks, although can occur for longer. The most
common symptom is watery diarrhoea. Other symptoms include
stomach cramps, dehydration, nausea and vomiting and fever.
E Coli 0157 is a relatively rare cause of infective diarrhoea in England.
Symptoms range from mild gastroenteritis through to severe bloody
diarrhoea. It can be associated with haemolytic uraemic syndrome and
thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura.
Giardia is causes by the protozoon parasite Giardia lamblia. Symptoms
include diarrhoea, foul smelling flatulence and abdominal cramps.
Symptoms typically last between 2-4 weeks, but chronic diarrhoea and
malabsorption can occur.
The patient has likely got a very low CD4+ count, due to his non-
compliance with medication and follow up and history of recurrent
pneumonia. CMV colitis with rectal and oesophageal involvement would
explain the tenesmus, odynophagia, along with the bloody diarrhoea,
abdominal cramps and weight loss.
Cryptosporidiosis and giardia do not tend to cause bloody diarrhoea.
Clostridium difficile is an important cause of diarrhoea in
immunocompromised patients. However, neither clostridium difficule
nor E Coli 0157 this would not explain the odynophagia or tenesmus.

Tigecycline is the correct answer. The patient has developed pneumonia
and sepsis secondary to infection with Klebsiella pneumoniae , which has
been identified as a carbapenemase-producing organism. This is a class
of bacteria known as carbapenemase-producing enterobacteriaceae.
These are gram-negative bacteria that are resistant to carbapenem and
extended-spectrum cephalosporin antibiotics. Effective antibiotics
against this class of bacteria include polymyxins (e.g. colistin),
tigecycline, fosfomycin or aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin). Risk
factors for CPE infection include immunosuppression (e.g. diabetes) and
previous hospital admission.

medication. This is effective against a wide variety of gram-negative and

Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. This has a wide spectrum of activity against
various gram-negative and gram-positive aerobes but is not effective
against CPE.

Which virus is likely to be responsible for these lesions?
explanation:
This is a description of AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is a disease of blood vessels that was considered very
rare before the start of the AIDS pandemic. AIDS is due to infection with
human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
There are four types of Kaposi sarcoma:
The classic type of Kaposi sarcoma affects elderly men of
Mediterranean and Middle European descent and in men in Sub-
Saharan Africa.
AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma.
Endemic or African Kaposi sarcoma arises in some parts of Africa
in children and young adults.
Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is due to drug treatment causing
immune suppression.
Classic Kaposi sarcoma is rare and unassociated with HIV infection. It
most often arises in middle-aged to elderly men of Mediterranean or
Jewish descent (less than 10% are women), particularly if they come
from a rural environment. They have a higher than expected rate of
diabetes mellitus.
AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma, unlike other forms of the disease, tends to
have an aggressive clinical course. It is the most common presentation
of Kaposi sarcoma. It has become less common in the US and Europe
because of effective HAART treatment for HIV disease.
Kaposi's sarcoma - caused by HHV-8 (human herpes virus 8)
Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by infection with human herpesvirus 8
(HHV8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV)
or KS agent
Typical histologic findings include proliferation of spindle cells,
prominent slit-like vascular spaces, intracellular hyaline bodies and
extravasated red blood cells.

Skin biopsy
Granulomatous dermatitis with inflammatory infiltrate

explanation:
This patient has an infection with the bacterium Mycobacterium
marinum, a species of mycobacteria commonly contracted through
Fish tank granuloma is caused by Mycobacterium marinum
exposure to swimming pool water or contact with fish e.g. through fish
tanks. This patient is a pet shop owner and has likely contracted the
illness through occupational exposure. Notably, in such patients, the
dominant hand is most frequently affected. After a 3-4 week incubation
period, a single lump or pustule appears that breaks down to form a
crusted lesion. The knuckles are commonly affected and a biopsy of the
lesion demonstrates granulomatous dermatitis and inflammatory
infiltrate within the dermis. Treatment is with antibiotics e.g. doxycycline.
Human papilloma virus (HPV) is a common cause of viral warts that are
commonly located on the cutaneous surface (e.g. hands, knees and
feet) or genitalia. Common warts found on the hands (also known as
verruca vulgaris) are hyperkeratotic, rough and papillomatous lesions.
However, on dermoscopy, multiple papillary capillaries can be visualised
rather than granulomatous dermatitis with inflammatory infiltrate.
Mycobacterium leprae causes leprosy. Symptoms of leprosy include
hypopigmented patches of skin associated with sensory loss. The areas
of skin affected by the disease are not limited by exposure, in contrast to
this patient's presentation.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause cutaneous symptoms such as
tuberculous gumma from the haematogenous spread of disease, lupus
vulgaris and miliary tuberculosis where there are multiple millet-sized
red skin lesions. These lesions are not seen in this patient and there is
no other history to suggest underlying tuberculosis.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is implicated in skin infections such as
external otitis or hot tub folliculitis (acquired from chlorinated hot tubs).
Infection is particularly more common in the immunocompromised and
is unlikely to be the causative pathogen in this case.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) related Posttransplant Lymphoproliferative Disease
explanation:
CMV infection is the correct answer. The presentation of fever,
diarrhoea, and malaise, coupled with the characteristic basophilic
CMV infection shows intranuclear inclusion bodies on histological
examination
intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (owl's eye
appearance) and the early post-transplant period (6 weeks), makes CMV
infection most likely. Prompt antiviral therapy with ganciclovir or
valganciclovir is essential. The leucopenia in case 2.9 may be attributed
to mycophenolate mofetil use.
Clostridioides difficile infection presents with profuse diarrhoea, often in
association with antibiotic use. Stool toxin or PCR testing confirms the
diagnosis. Histologically, pseudomembranous colitis is seen,
characterised by volcano-like fibrinopurulent exudates. In contrast to
CMV, no inclusion bodies are observed.
EBV-related post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) usually
occurs later in the ≥ 6 months post-transplant. It is more often
associated with systemic lymphadenopathy or mass lesions than
isolated colonic ulcerations. Histologically, it shows lymphoid
proliferation without viral inclusions. PTLD is treated by reducing
immunosuppression and initiating anti-CD20 therapy (e.g., rituximab).
Microsporidiosis typically presents later post-transplant in patients with
prolonged or profound immunosuppression. It causes chronic diarrhoea
and weight loss. Diagnosis is based on histology, which shows small
cytoplasmic spores using modified trichrome or acid-fast staining.
Unlike CMV, microsporidia do not cause intranuclear inclusions, and
antiviral treatments are ineffective.
Mycophenolate-induced colitis can mimic CMV clinically, presenting
with watery diarrhoea and abdominal symptoms. However, histology
shows crypt apoptosis without viral inclusions, and CMV PCR is
negative. Symptoms improve with dose reduction or cessation of
mycophenolate. In this case, characteristic intranuclear inclusions
support CMV colitis as the most likely diagnosis.

diabetes and peripheral vascular disease rather than hypertension.

development of necrotizing fasciitis but he drinks within normal limits
(i.e. < 14 units/week).

What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
explanation:
The clinical history is suggestive of cutaneous larva migrans which is
caused by infection of the dog hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense.
Management is with albendazole or ivermectin.
Flucloxacillin and doxycycline are indicated for cellulitis.
Clotrimazole and terbinafine are used in the treatment of fungal
infections such as ringworm.
Albendazole is the treatment of choice for cutaneous larva migrans

isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, with pyridoxine supplements.
Eight weeks later, culture results show that the Mycobacterium
tuberculosis is resistant to isoniazid. What should his further treatment
regime be?
options: Four months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, with pyridoxine supplements
Four months of rifampicin and ethambutol, with pyridoxine supplements
Four months of rifampicin and ethambutol
explanation:
In fully sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, after two
months, the pyrazinamide and ethambutol are stopped and rifampicin
and isoniazid (with pyridoxine support) are continued for a further four
months. However, in cases of confirmed isoniazid resistance, rifampicin
and ethambutol are continued for the further 4 months of treatment, with
discontinuation of the isoniazid (and supportive pyridoxine) and
pyrazinamide.
In confirmed isoniazid resistance, ethambutol is continued for 6
months of treatment
This is not multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (does not respond to at least
isoniazid and rifampicin), so it is not appropriate to add a quinolone or
aminoglycoside.

system (CNS) will most influence choice of drug therapy. Pentamidine is
the treatment of choice in early infection, while choices for CNS infection
include suramin, melarsoprol, eflornithine and nifurtimox. These
medications are not widely available and can result in extremely severe
side effects, so are only prescribed by tropical medicine specialists.
Trypanosomiasis
Two main form of this protozoal disease are recognised - African
trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) and American trypanosomiasis
(Chagas' disease).

immunoglobulin administration.

She has no past medical history and takes no regular tablets apart from
the oral contraceptive pill. She has no allergies apart from peanuts. She
has a been suffering from diarrhoea for three days with mild abdominal
cramps which started five days after returning from her trip. There has
been a small amount of blood in her stool. Her observations are within
normal range. She has no postural symptoms. Stool samples are
requested and sent to the microbiology lab. What is the most
appropriate treatment?
Ciprofloxacin
Tetracycline
Oral rehydration solution
Metronidazole
Co-amoxiclav
Question 9 of 287
A 25-year-old woman returns from a holiday in Thailand with diarrhoea.
She has no past medical history and takes no regular tablets apart from
the oral contraceptive pill. She has no allergies apart from peanuts. She
has a been suffering from diarrhoea for three days with mild abdominal
cramps which started five days after returning from her trip. There has
been a small amount of blood in her stool. Her observations are within
normal range. She has no postural symptoms. Stool samples are
requested and sent to the microbiology lab. What is the most
appropriate treatment?
explanation:
The correct answer is oral rehydration solution. Empirical antibiotics are
only indicated if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or if elderly,
even if the patient has bloody diarrhoea. CIprofloxacin is used to treat
Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter, tetracycline can be used for
cholera, metronidazole in parasitic infections or other bowel problems,
and finally, co-amoxiclav is seldom used in enteric infections.

Question 10 of 287
A 14 month-old Syrian girl is brought to the health centre by her mother.
They are living in a Jordanian refugee camp after fleeing violence in their
country. She has a widespread maculopapular rash that first affected the
face before spreading to the torso and limbs. On examination, she has a
cough, rhinorrhoea and conjunctivitis bilaterally. White spotting is seen
on her buccal mucosa. The mother reports that her other children have
had similar symptoms.
Which is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation:
The child has a classical case of measles, showing signs of the three C's
(Cough, Coryza & Conjunctivits). Although usually self limiting, measles
can have severe consequences. All children in developing countries
should receive two dose of vitamin A. This replenishes the low levels of
vitamin A caused be measles which can lead on to diarrhoea, corneal
perforation and secondary bacterial pneumonia. Vitamin A has been
shown to reduce deaths from measles by 50%.
Passive immunity from maternal antibodies protects infants under the
age of 1 from measles.

On examination, he appears cachectic. There are multiple, well-defined

with no palpable masses.

A 49-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit with a 2-week
history of pain and difficulty when swallowing. He reports having lost
approximately 2-3kg in weight from reduced oral intake. His past
medical history includes previous hospital admissions for lower
respiratory tract infections and lower limb deep vein thrombosis.
On examination, he appears cachectic. There are multiple, well-defined
white plaques over the oral mucosa. His abdomen is soft and non-tender
with no palpable masses.
CD4 count

What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
This patient has a diagnosis of oesophageal candidiasis given the
classical history of painful swallowing and visible white mucosal
plaques on examination. It is particularly more common in
immunocompromised individuals (e.g. such as patients with HIV). The
treatment of choice for treating candidiasis in immunocompromised
Candidiasis in immunocompromised patients should be treated
using high dose fluconazole
patients is with high-dose fluconazole or itraconazole.
Aciclovir is used to treat viral infections, including herpes simplex and
herpes zoster. Typically viral rashes such as herpes simplex present with
ulceration or vesicles. The presence of a white mucosal coating in an
immunocompromised patient is highly suggestive of candidiasis, for
which antifungal medication is needed, rather than antivirals like
aciclovir.
Caspofungin is not a first-line treatment for oesophageal candidiasis. It
is reserved for cases of refractory disease that do not respond to initial
treatment with fluconazole. As first-line therapy has not yet been
initiated, it would be inappropriate to start the patient on more invasive
treatment such as caspofungin.
Co-amoxiclav and metronidazole would be indicated if there were
concerns that this patient was suffering from a bacterial infection.
However, the classical history of odynophagia and white mucosal
coating in an immunocompromised patient makes candidiasis much
more likely to be the diagnosis.
Nystatin and chlorhexidine mouthwash would normally form part of the
initial management in immunocompetent patients. However, this patient
has a CD4 count of < 100 cells/mm³ suggesting significant
immunocompromise. Therefore, stronger treatment such as high-dose
fluconazole is needed.

disease clinic. He was feeling tired and generally unwell over several
weeks since last visiting Nigeria, his country of origin. He has also
travelled for business to the United States six months ago. He has had
fever and rigors as well as headaches. Posterior lymph nodes have been
present and have been aspirated one week ago, and trypomastigotes
were present. What is the most likely causative organism?
Trypanosoma rhodesiense
Trypanosoma gambiense
Trypanosoma cruzi
Leishmania mexicana
Leishmania tropica
Question 13 of 287
A 42-year-old immigrant from Nigeria has been referred to the infectious
disease clinic. He was feeling tired and generally unwell over several
weeks since last visiting Nigeria, his country of origin. He has also
travelled for business to the United States six months ago. He has had
fever and rigors as well as headaches. Posterior lymph nodes have been
present and have been aspirated one week ago, and trypomastigotes
were present. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is Trypanosoma gambiense. This is a patient with a
clinical history suggestive of African trypanosomiasis with a slow
wasting course. The presence of trypomastigotes means that there will
be a Trypanosoma infection. The species can be determined by
geography. Rhodesiense occurs in east Africa whilst gambiense occurs
in west Africa, including Nigeria. Uganda is the only country with both.
Cruzi is endemic in South America and causes American
trypanosomiasis. Leishmania are other protozoa occurring in Africa,
South America and India.

he has been acting strangely for a number of weeks and complaining of

partner refuses to be tested as he does not believe in 'medical lies'.
On admission he is apyrexial with a blood pressure of 114/82mmHg and
pulse 78/min.

A 33-year-old man who has recently emigrated from Zimbabwe is
admitted after being found confused at home. His partner reports that
he has been acting strangely for a number of weeks and complaining of
altered taste and dizziness. She reports that she is HIV positive but her
partner refuses to be tested as he does not believe in 'medical lies'.
On admission he is apyrexial with a blood pressure of 114/82mmHg and
pulse 78/min.
Rapid HIV testing confirms that he has the infection. His CD4 count is 11
cells/µl.
An MRI (T1 C+) shows the following:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
Other than starting highly active antiretroviral treatment, what is the
most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
The correct answer in this case is sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine. The
patient's presentation with confusion, altered taste, dizziness, and a low
CD4 count of 11 cells/µl suggests that he has an opportunistic infection
due to his HIV infection. The MRI image provided shows multiple ring-
enhancing lesions, which are consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis.
Cerebral toxoplasmosis is caused by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma
gondii and is a common opportunistic infection in patients with
advanced HIV disease. The recommended treatment for cerebral
toxoplasmosis is a combination of sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine.
Amphotericin B is an antifungal medication used primarily to treat
invasive fungal infections such as cryptococcal meningitis or
disseminated histoplasmosis. Although these infections can occur in
patients with HIV, the MRI findings and clinical presentation are more
suggestive of cerebral toxoplasmosis.
Surgical resection might be considered for space-occupying lesions
such as brain abscesses or tumours. However, given the patient's
multiple ring-enhancing lesions on MRI and low CD4 count, cerebral
toxoplasmosis is much more likely than a primary brain tumour or
abscesses.
HIV, neuro symptoms, multiple brain lesions with ring enhancement
- toxoplasmosis
Steroids + methotrexate + whole brain irradiation would be a treatment
approach for primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, which
can also present with neurological symptoms in patients with HIV.
However, CNS lymphoma typically presents as a solitary lesion rather
than multiple ring-enhancing lesions seen in this case.
Rifampicin + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + ethambutol + steroids
represent the standard regimen for treating tuberculosis (TB). While TB
can involve the CNS in patients with HIV, the MRI findings are not typical
for CNS TB. Moreover, the patient's symptoms of altered taste and
dizziness do not fit well with a diagnosis of CNS TB.

A 44-year-old woman with a background of asthma who has required
frequent use of oral corticosteroids is inquiring about vaccinations
available to her. Which one of the following should be recommended?
options: 23-valent unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine and influenza vaccine
13-valent conjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine and influenza vaccine
explanation:
Patients with chronic respiratory conditions including asthma requiring
frequent use of oral steroids should be offered both the 23-valent
unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine and the influenza
vaccine. In this population, the pneumococcal vaccine is usually given as
a once off but may be required 5 yearly depending on the underlying
condition and the age of the patient. The influenza vaccine, however, is
given annually.
The 13-valent conjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is
routinely given to infants as it has been found to be more effective given
their less mature immune systems.

days after returning from Sao Paulo. She noted that fevers and
generalised abdominal pain started the day before she boarded her flight
home and that the rash had come up in the last 24 hours.
On examination, the woman has petechiae and a maculopapular rash
over her wrists, ankles, and palms as well as a single itchy, erythematous
raised papule with a central punctum on her right calf.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate treatment?
Albendazole
Artemether with lumefantrine
Doxycycline
Metronidazole
Praziquantel
Question 16 of 287
A 23-year-old woman attends with fever, myalgia, rash, and headache 4
days after returning from Sao Paulo. She noted that fevers and
generalised abdominal pain started the day before she boarded her flight
home and that the rash had come up in the last 24 hours.
On examination, the woman has petechiae and a maculopapular rash
over her wrists, ankles, and palms as well as a single itchy, erythematous
raised papule with a central punctum on her right calf.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis here is Rocky Mountain spotted fever, one of
the Rickettsial diseases. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is transmitted via
tick bites in endemic areas such as South America - the single, itchy,
erythematous, raised papule is descriptive of a tick bite. It presents
initially with general symptoms of malaise, fever, and abdominal pain.
The classic vasculitic rash then develops after 3-5 days.
Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
Doxycycline is typically used in the management of typhus
Albendazole is incorrect. This would be more appropriate for helminth
infections such as roundworm and hookworm.
Artemether with lumefantrine is incorrect. This would be the appropriate
treatment for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. P. falciparum malaria
is most prevalent in Africa rather than in South America. It can present
with similar general symptoms to Rocky Mountain spotted fever with
fevers, headache, and myalgias but is also often associated with
hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. It is not typically associated with the
vasculitic rash seen in this patient.
Metronidazole is incorrect. It has good action against anaerobic bacteria
and protozoa but would not be the choice for Rickettsial infections.
Praziquantel is incorrect. This is used to treat parasitic worm infections
such as schistosomiasis. It would not be the choice for Rickettsial
infections.

explanation:
Care must be taken when interpreting syphilis investigations. Cardiolipin
tests (e.g. VDRL and RPR) are non-specific and can be positive in many
diseases such as TB, malaria and HIV. Treponemal specific antibody
tests (e.g. TPHA) are very specific to Treponema, however the species
Treponemal specific antibody tests (e.g. TPHA) are very specific to
Treponema but not necessarily syphillis, as the species Treponema
can cause a variety of diseases including syphilis, yaws and pinta
Treponema can cause a variety of diseases including syphilis, yaws and
pinta.
Yaws is a chronic infection that affects mainly the skin, bone and
cartilage. The disease occurs mainly in low socio-economic
communities in tropical areas of Africa, Asia and Latin America. The
causative organism is a bacterium called Treponema pertenue, a
subspecies of Treponema pallidum that causes venereal syphilis.
However, yaws is a non-venereal infection.
In primary yaws, a single skin lesion develops at the point of entry of the
bacterium after 2-4 weeks. This nodule can break down into an
exudative ulcer. Without treatment, secondary yaws can occur, resulting
in multiple lesions appear all over the body, more commonly over the
face, trunk, genitalia and buttocks. Later on in the disease course,
widespread bone, joint and soft tissue destruction can occur.

Serological testing is the correct answer. The diagnosis is leptospirosis,
as evidenced by a history of fever, myalgia, headache and
subconjunctival haemorrhage in association with hepatorenal failure in a
patient with a potential geographic exposure to infected urine
(freshwater exposure). The most commonly used test to diagnose
leptospirosis is serological testing for IgM antibodies to leptospirosis.
The disadvantages with this method of investigation are false positives,
the inability for the test to diagnose early infection and the fact that
antibodies can persist in the sera for months after initial infection,
making interpretation of timing of infection difficult in cases of
diagnostic uncertainty. Antibodies are not usually present until the
infection has been present for seven days. In this case, the patient has
presented with eight days of symptoms and therefore antibody testing
should be positive.
Serology is the most commonly used test for the diagnosis of
leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not be present until after 7
days
Blood culture is the wrong answer. Culture testing for leptospirosis can
take up to three months and is therefore predominantly used for
retrospective diagnosis.
Urine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing is incorrect. While this
technique is effective in identifying leptospira infection, it is not as
commonly used as serological testing as its use is precluded by cost
and technical factors in non-reference laboratories.
Urinary antigen testing is incorrect. This is used to diagnose
pneumococcal and legionella pneumonia infections. The clinical history
is not suggestive of a pneumonia.
Urine culture is incorrect. The use of this method of testing is precluded
by the fact that cultures may take 8-12 weeks to form.

explanation:
Panton-Valentine Leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin which is produced
by staphylococcus aureus. It has an affinity for white blood cells and the
endothelium. Clinically PVL will often present with a necrotising
pneumonia, characterised by severe bilateral pneumonia with cavitations
on X-ray. Often patients presenting will have a history of boils or necrotic
skin lesions. As the staphylococcus is easily transmitted there may be a
recent family history of similar infections / boils.
Although all of the answers in this stem could be associated with
cavitating pneumonia, the severity of the clinical presentation and
history of boils in the family points towards a PVL-pneumonia.

© Image used on license from Radiopaedia

explanation:
The key to answering this question is to look at the history rather than
the x-ray. A combination of HIV + chest symptoms + unremarkable
auscultatory findings in an exam are highly suggestive of Pneumocystis
jiroveci pneumonia (more commonly known as PCP). X-ray changes in
Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia are generally too subtle for non-
radiologists to detect. The x-ray should however help you to exclude
some of the other diagnoses.
The chest x-ray shows hazy, perihilar mid and upper zone opacification
with some interstitial prominence. A few discrete cysts (termed
pneumatocoeles) measuring up to 1cm are present. The presence of
pneumatocoeles in a HIV patient suggests Pneumocystis jiroveci
pneumonia.

explanation:
Human herpes virus 5 (HHV 5), is cytomegalovirus (CMV). In patients
who are post-transplant, CMV infections can occur from reactivation of
latent infection, infection via the transplanted organ, or because of a new
primary infection. Treatment is with IV ganciclovir, and where there is
ganciclovir resistance, foscarnet or cidofovir are alternative options.
Without treatment, further deterioration in renal function is the likely
outcome.
IV acyclovir is the usual treatment option for herpes simplex or herpes
zoster infection and oral valaciclovir is an alternative option to oral
acyclovir for the long term treatment of herpes simplex. Lamivudine is
used in the treatment of HIV/AIDs and hepatitis B infection.
Valganciclovir is an alternative oral option to IV ganciclovir with potential
use for CMV prophylaxis.

A 44-year-old man presents with a 1 day history of fever. He returned to
the UK 12 days ago after visiting his family in northern Uganda. He has
been resident in the UK for the last 20 years and returns home on
average once a year. He does not routinely take malaria prophylaxis.
On examination his temperature is 39.4ºC, pulse is 86 beats per minute,
his blood pressure is 115/78 mmHg and his oxygen saturations are 98%
on air. The remainder of the physical examination is normal. A thick and
thin blood film are sent to the lab which confirms Plasmodium falciparum
malaria. The report reads 2.1% parasitaemia with the presence of
schizonts.
What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
Intravenous artesunate
Oral quinine sulfate
Oral chloroquine
Oral atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone)
Intravenous quinine
Question 24 of 287
A 44-year-old man presents with a 1 day history of fever. He returned to
the UK 12 days ago after visiting his family in northern Uganda. He has
been resident in the UK for the last 20 years and returns home on
average once a year. He does not routinely take malaria prophylaxis.
On examination his temperature is 39.4ºC, pulse is 86 beats per minute,
his blood pressure is 115/78 mmHg and his oxygen saturations are 98%
on air. The remainder of the physical examination is normal. A thick and
thin blood film are sent to the lab which confirms Plasmodium falciparum
malaria. The report reads 2.1% parasitaemia with the presence of
schizonts.
What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
explanation:
This question examines your ability to differentiate severe malaria from
uncomplicated malaria and then apply the correct therapy.
We are told the patient has been living in the UK for the last 20 years. As
a result any natural immunity built up in earlier life would have
dramatically reduced putting him at high risk of developing severe
malaria with a relatively low level parasitaemia.
The most important information given is that schizonts are present in
the blood film. Schizonts are the final step before red blood cells rupture
and release more parasites (merozoites) into the blood.
Given his lack of immunity and an impending rise in parasitaemia it
would be pertinent to consider this a case of severe malaria and treat
accordingly with intravenous therapy early on. This excludes answers B,
C and D. Furthermore chloroquine is only used routinely in the treatment
of non falciparum malaria.
WHO guidelines recommend the use of intravenous artesunate for at
least the first 24 hours until the patient can tolerate oral medication.

A 38-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department complaining
of feeling unwell. He complained of a headache that had been present
for the last two days which he described a continuous ache worse in the
morning, as well as a sore throat. He later developed diarrhoea, opening
his bowels three times per day passing watery loose stool. Since then he
has deteriorated, complaining of nausea and vomiting on the day of
admission. He also noted a new rash on his chest which developed over
the last few hours and complained of pains in his muscles. He had
returned two weeks ago from a six-month backpacking expedition
around Africa and Far East Asia; he was prescribed doxycycline as
antimalarial prophylaxis but had discontinued them two weeks into his
trip after suffering from severe sunburns. He had not taken
recommended vaccinations prior to his trip as he was engaged with
work commitments. His past medical history comprised of asthma and
depression for which he was prescribed sertraline 100mg OD and Clenil
modulite 2 puffs BD.

The Viral Haemorrhagic Fevers describe infection by a group of RNA
viruses which include Yellow fever, Lassa fever and Ebola virus. Given
the current outbreak in West Africa, this group of infections must be
considered as a differential in returning travellers presenting with a fever.
They are characterised by initially non-specific symptoms such as fever,
headache, vomiting, sore throat, diarrhoea and myalgic muscle pains,
progressing to shock, renal failure and the presence of disseminated

supportive care and early diagnosis is imperative. There are of course
many differentials, malaria being a key one here, but the absence of
parasites on thick film make this a less likely diagnosis.

The GP has requested a follow-up blood test which is shown below.

Hb

WBC
1.9 * 10 /l
Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
explanation:
It is likely she has received a protracted course of antibiotics, possibly
more than one different antibiotic even.
An important side effect of azathioprine is cytopaenia. Azathioprine is
metabolised to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) and then inactivated either by
oxidation or methylation. Oxidation is catalysed by xanthine oxidase and
methylation is catalysed by the enzyme TPMT. Factors that can lead to
elevated levels of azathioprine are:
Drugs that inhibit xanthine oxidase e.g. allopurinol
Drugs that can also cause myelosuppression e.g.sulphonamides,
trimethoprim
Reduced activity of TPMT
Trimethoprim
Trimethoprim is an antibiotic, mainly used in the management of urinary
tract infections.
Mechanism of action
interferes with DNA synthesis by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase
may, therefore, interact with methotrexate, which also inhibits
dihydrofolate reductase
Adverse effects
myelosuppression
transient rise in creatinine: trimethoprim competitively inhibits the
tubular secretion of creatinine resulting in a temporary increase
which reverses upon stopping the drug
trimethoprim blocks the ENaC channel in the distal nephron,
causing a hyperkalaemic distal RTA (type 4). It also inhibits
creatinine secretion, often leading to an increase in creatinine
by around 40 points (but not necessarily causing AKI)

Genitourinary clinic.
As part of his routine HIV work up his HLA B*5701 result is reported as
positive.
Which drug will not be included in his ART regimen as a result of this
information?
Tenofovir
Emtricitabine
Lamivudine
Stavudine
Abacavir
Question 27 of 287
A 45 year old man is diagnosed with HIV following attendance at
Genitourinary clinic.
As part of his routine HIV work up his HLA B*5701 result is reported as
positive.
Which drug will not be included in his ART regimen as a result of this
information?
explanation:
Abacavir can cause a severe and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity
reaction. It is a cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction which
occurs around 6 weeks after starting treatment. Symptoms are of fever,
rash, malaise and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Patients without HLA B*5701 are highly unlikely to develop
hypersensitivity. Those with the HLA B*5701 allele have a 50% risk and
therefore in these individuals abacavir should be avoided.
It is therefore routine to test HLA B*5701 status on all newly diagnosed
patients with HIV.

A 28 year-old man presents to his doctor with a rash and bone pain.
Radiographs of the limbs revealed numerous osteolytic lesions. He was
successfully treated for secondary syphilis.
Which of the following tests is likely to remain positive in this patient
despite treatment?
Blood culture
Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA)
Venereal disease reference laboratory (VDRL)
Rapid plasmin reagin (RPR)
Wasserman test
Question 29 of 287
A 28 year-old man presents to his doctor with a rash and bone pain.
Radiographs of the limbs revealed numerous osteolytic lesions. He was
successfully treated for secondary syphilis.
Which of the following tests is likely to remain positive in this patient
despite treatment?
explanation:
Syphilis is a disease caused by infection with the spirochete Treponema
pallidum. The infection is systemic and the disease is characterized by
periods of latency. These features, together with the fact that Treponema
pallidum cannot be isolated in culture, mean that serologic techniques
play a major role in the diagnosis and follow-up of treatment for syphilis.
The Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (also called TPPA
test) is an indirect agglutination assay used for detection and titration of
antibodies against Treponema pallidum.
IgG antibodies to syphilis can remain elevated despite appropriate
antimicrobial treatment and a reactive result does not distinguish
between recent or past infection.

37.6°C
On mobilisation, his saturations reduce to 88%.
Chest X-ray is clear.
What investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
explanation:
The correct answer is broncho-alveolar lavage which is most likely to be
able to demonstrate PCP characteristic cysts with silver staining. There
are several factors highly suggestive of PCP. This gentleman is poorly
compliant with his HIV medication and the other medication regime he is
describing is PCP prophylaxis, suggesting a low CD4 count. He also is
tachypnoeic with low saturations on mobilising and a clear chest X-ray.
All of these factors suggest PCP. In the case of a productive cough,
sputum could be obtained without the need for a broncho-alveolar
lavage. Imaging can be suggestive of PCP but is not as sensitive or
diagnostic as broncho-alveolar lavage. ECG and echocardiogram have
no role in PCP diagnosis.
Source:
Nelson, M., Dh Dockrell, and S. Edwards. 'British HIV Association and
British Infection Association Guidelines for the Treatment of
Opportunistic Infection in HIV-seropositive Individuals 2011.' HIV
Medicine 12 (2011): 1-5.

been getting worse for the past two months and he now complains that
he is 'bent over'. Over the past three months he describes feeling
generally unwell, with a poor appetite and night sweats.

is the most appropriate plan for the nurse?
options: Admit to hospital for IV antibiotics
Advise that the risk of transmission is not significant
explanation:
This is a patient who has had a close contact with respiratory secretions
of a person with confirmed meningococcal meningitis. Despite the fact
that she has not had prolonged exposure, prophylaxis in the form of oral
ciprofloxacin is needed.
People who have been exposed to a patient with confirmed
bacterial meningitis should be given prophylactic antibiotics if they
been exposed to respiratory secretion, regardless of closeness of
contact
The risk of transmission by this route is sufficiently significant to make
monitoring for symptoms or not giving any treatment inappropriate.
A lumbar puncture is unlikely to be a helpful investigation for her as it
cannot exclude that she will develop meningitis.
IV antibiotics are used to treat meningitis, whilst oral antibiotics can be
used for prophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis.

Of note, he returned from Afghanistan two weeks ago. Examination
reveals a temperature of 38.1ºC, heart rate 89/min, blood pressure
123/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min and oxygen saturations of 99%.
There is no evidence of no neck stiffness, objective photophobia,
jaundice or splenomegaly.

Chikungunya

Plasmodium falciparum

Question 34 of 287
A 19-year-old man attends the Emergency department with a fever for
the past one week. He notes that the fever comes on alternate days. He
reports also a co-existing headache, but no other particular symptoms.
Of note, he returned from Afghanistan two weeks ago. Examination
reveals a temperature of 38.1ºC, heart rate 89/min, blood pressure
123/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min and oxygen saturations of 99%.
There is no evidence of no neck stiffness, objective photophobia,
jaundice or splenomegaly.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fever in the returning traveller is a common presentation in the
Emergency department. A knowledge of the areas travelled and
incubation periods is essential to accurately diagnosing the potential
infectious disease.
Chikungunya is a viral disease transmitted to humans via infected
mosquitos. Fever and joint pain is the mos common presentation. The
incubation period is 2-12 days.
Zika virus is currently not present in Afghanistan.
Dengue fever has a incubation period of 4-10 days.
This leaves plasmodium falciparum, which has a usual incubation of 7-
14 days (but up to 3 months), and plasmodium vivax which has a typical
incubation of 12-17 days (but reported up to 12 months) following
exposure. Factors that point away from p. falciparum are the milder
presentation and the much lower prevalence of it in Afghanistan (p.
falciparum 5%, p. vivax 95%). Furthermore, fever due to malaria on
alternate days, known as benign tertian malaria, is suggestive of either p.
vivax or p. ovale. Comparatively, p. falciparum will typically cause more
of a continuous fever.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension,
who is currently taking metformin and lisinopril, presents to the
Emergency Department with a one-week history of dysuria, increased
urinary frequency, and lower abdominal discomfort. She denies
experiencing flank pain, nausea, or vomiting. On examination, her
temperature is 38.2 ºC, and she exhibits suprapubic tenderness.
Initial urinalysis demonstrates pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and
nitrites. She was commenced on oral ciprofloxacin; however, her urinary
symptoms have persisted, and she has developed recurrent fevers.
Subsequent urine culture reveals an ESBL-producing E. coli infection.
What is the most appropriate next step in managing this woman's
condition?
Continue ciprofloxacin
Switch to aztreonam
Switch to ceftazidime
Switch to meropenem
Switch to piperacillin-tazobactam
Question 35 of 287
A 56-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension,
who is currently taking metformin and lisinopril, presents to the
Emergency Department with a one-week history of dysuria, increased
urinary frequency, and lower abdominal discomfort. She denies
experiencing flank pain, nausea, or vomiting. On examination, her
temperature is 38.2 ºC, and she exhibits suprapubic tenderness.
Initial urinalysis demonstrates pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and
nitrites. She was commenced on oral ciprofloxacin; however, her urinary
symptoms have persisted, and she has developed recurrent fevers.
Subsequent urine culture reveals an ESBL-producing E. coli infection.
What is the most appropriate next step in managing this woman's
condition?
explanation:
Switch to meropenem is the correct answer. The clinical presentation
and urine analysis indicate a urinary tract infection that has not
responded to ciprofloxacin therapy. The urine culture has confirmed the
presence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing E.coli,
Carbapenems (e.g. meropenem) are useful in the management of
ESBL-producing bacteria
which demonstrates resistance to a range of antibiotics, including
quinolones such as ciprofloxacin, third-generation cephalosporins like
ceftazidime, and penicillins including amoxicillin and ampicillin. Among
the options provided, meropenem is the preferred treatment. This
antibiotic is part of the beta-lactam class within the carbapenems
subgroup and is effective against ESBL-producing organisms like ESBL-
producing E.coli.
Continue ciprofloxacin is unsuitable given that there has been no initial
response to this drug, coupled with emerging resistance in ESBL-
producing bacteria. Ciprofloxacin belongs to the fluoroquinolone family,
primarily targeting gram-negative and atypical bacteria, with some
activity against gram-positive species.
Switch to aztreonam is an incorrect option. Aztreonam, a monobactam,
is hydrolysed by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), rendering
it ineffective against most ESBL-producing organisms unless combined
with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (BLI) such as avibactam. Studies have
shown that ESBL-producing E. coli exhibits high resistance to aztreonam
monotherapy, with resistance rates exceeding 90% in some reports.
Therefore, aztreonam alone is not suitable for treating infections caused
by ESBL-producing E. coli.
Switch to piperacillin-tazobactam is an incorrect choice. It falls under
the extended-spectrum penicillin antibiotic category (a part of beta-
lactams). While it may work for ESBL-producing E.coli, guidelines
generally prioritise carbapenems (such as meropenem) for complicated
or treatment-refractory ESBL infections to ensure a robust clinical cure.
Switch to ceftazidime is ineffective against ESBL-producing bacteria. It
is a third-generation cephalosporin with anti-pseudomonal properties.
Notably, ceftazidime-avibactam – a newer agent within this class – has
some efficacy against ESBL-producing pathogens.

and she is visibly coryzal. Her chest is clear to auscultation. Her chest X-

been closed to visitors due to an Influenza outbreak. Which of the

Empirical antibiotics for pneumonia
Zanamivir
Oseltamivir
Ribavirin
Salbutamol nebulisers
Question 37 of 287
An 81-year-old nursing home resident presents with a 48-hour history of
pyrexia, myalgia and coryza. On examination, her temperature is 37.9ºC
and she is visibly coryzal. Her chest is clear to auscultation. Her chest X-
ray is clear. Her relatives inform you that the nursing home has recently
been closed to visitors due to an Influenza outbreak. Which of the
following drugs should you also consider adding?
explanation:
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is the first-line treatment recommended for
patients with suspected or confirmed Influenza A. Ribavirin has not be
shown to be efficacious in the management of influenza. Zanamivir is
useful in patients with a poor swallow or in those with suspected or
confirmed exposure to oseltamivir-resistant influenza.
Her chest X-ray is clear and therefore there is no role for the addition of
antibiotic therapy at this stage.
Salbutamol nebulisers can be useful in patients with wheeze, however,
appropriate isolation precautions should be secured prior to the
administration of nebulisers in patients with Influenza infection.

What treatment is recommended first-line for this condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is ivermectin. This patient is likely to have developed
strongyloidiasis, a parasitic infection caused by the nematode
Strongyloides stercoralis. This is a widely-distributed helminth but the
majority of cases are seen in sub-Saharan Africa and South America.
Infection is frequently asymptomatic and the first clue is peripheral
eosinophilia. In this case, the episode described in Malawi is consistent
with larva currens, a rash that develops when the worm penetrates the
skin before entering the bloodstream. From here they spread through the
lungs, over the epiglottis, are swallowed, and settle in the small intestine,
where they lay their eggs. Respiratory symptoms are rare but cough and
wheeze may develop during pulmonary migration. In chronic infection,
abdominal pain and diarrhoea may occur. In the context of
immunocompromise, Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome can occur,
presenting with bloody colitis and pneumonitis, often with pleural
effusions. The treatment of choice in all cases is ivermectin, although
albendazole and thiabendazole are alternatives.
Artemisinin combination therapy is incorrect. This is the treatment of
choice for most cases of uncomplicated malaria. Malaria does not tend
to cause eosinophilia or skin lesions, and she has been compliant with
prophylaxis. These factors suggest this is very unlikely to be the
diagnosis.
Melarsoprol is incorrect. This is an arsenic-based treatment option for
East African sleeping sickness, caused by Trypanosoma brucei
rhodesiense. This is a rapidly progressive form of sleeping sickness,
initially causing an influenza-like illness with arthralgia and
lymphadenopathy but quickly progressing to altered mental status and
death. Melarsoprol is associated with significant toxicity and would not
be used for strongyloidiasis.
Nifurtimox/eflornithine combination therapy is incorrect. This is a
treatment option for West African sleeping sickness, caused by the
protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. This causes a
slowly progressive illness characterised by behavioural change,
alterations to the sleep-wake cycle, and finally coma. There are no
symptoms here to suggest this and it is not typically associated with
Ivermectin is the drug of choice for treatment of strongyloidiasis
eosinophilia.
Praziquantel is incorrect. This is the treatment of choice for
schistosomiasis, a tapeworm infection caused by a variety of species of
schistosomes. The organism uses freshwater snails as an intermediate
host before being released into the water, where it penetrates human
skin and settles in the gastrointestinal or genito-urinary tract depending
on the species. There may be an itchy rash at the time of infection,
known as cercarial dermatitis, but this would not move up the limb or be
described as serpiginous. Schistosomiasis often presents with
eosinophilia, but in this case, the patient has been careful to avoid going
in the water, making this unlikely to be the cause.
Strongyloides stercoralis
Strongyloides stercoralis is a human parasitic nematode worm. The
larvae are present in soil and gain access to the body by penetrating the
skin. Infection with Strongyloides stercoralis causes strongyloidiasis.

history of fever, headache, and a rash. He describes the rash as initially
consisting of small red spots that have since coalesced into larger,
darker areas. He has recently returned from travelling in a rural region of
Southeast Asia. On physical examination, you note a black eschar on his
left ankle and a diffuse maculopapular rash across his trunk and
extremities.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Leptospirosis
Malaria
Rocky mountain spotted fever
Scrub typhus
Typhoid fever
Question 39 of 287
A 32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a five-day
history of fever, headache, and a rash. He describes the rash as initially
consisting of small red spots that have since coalesced into larger,
darker areas. He has recently returned from travelling in a rural region of
Southeast Asia. On physical examination, you note a black eschar on his
left ankle and a diffuse maculopapular rash across his trunk and
extremities.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scrub typhus is the correct diagnosis. The clinical picture of a 5-day
history of fever, headache, and a diffuse maculopapular rash involving
the trunk and extremities, in conjunction with a distinctive black eschar
on the left ankle, strongly suggests scrub typhus. This condition is an
endemic rickettsial infection in Southeast Asia caused by Orientia
tsutsugamushi, transmitted by larval mites, and targets endothelial cells.
Notably, less than 50% of patients exhibit an eschar at the site of the
mite bite. Untreated scrub typhus can be fatal. Doxycycline is the
treatment of choice.

Exposure to bats/caves is a risk factor for Marburg virus, which

viral hemorrhagic fever. This condition typically presents with an abrupt
onset of fever, headache and malaise and progresses to include
gastrointestinal symptoms, arthralgia/myalgia and subsequently
haemorrhagic complications with multi-organ dysfunction as evidenced
in this case. The incubation period before the onset of symptoms is
typically 3-10 days. In addition to the geographic and zoonotic risk
factors, it is the only diagnosis listed that could account for the
haemorrhagic complications in this scenario (oozing from venepuncture
sites and bleeding from mucosal membranes). Treatment is supportive
and the condition is associated with a high mortality rate.
Hepatitis A is incorrect. While this could account for jaundice and
transaminitis, it is typically a self-limiting illness and associated with
fulminant liver failure only in very rare cases. It is not associated with
haemorrhagic complications.
Leptospirosis is incorrect. While this condition can present with fever,
headache and liver dysfunction, the traditional vectors for transmission
are mice, rats, cows and pigs. It is transmitted classically by coming into
contact with infected urine. While it is associated with subconjunctival
haemorrhage, it is not usually associated with more diffuse
haemorrhage as seen in this case. It is treated with antibiotics.
Malaria is incorrect. While this is the most common cause of the fever in
the returning traveller, the patient has taken malaria prophylaxis and has
had negative testing for malaria in addition to experiencing
haemorrhagic complications, all of which make a diagnosis of malaria
unlikely.
Typhoid is incorrect. While this is a common cause of fever in the
returning traveller and is associated with fever and diarrhoea, it would
not account for the haemorrhagic complications detailed in this
scenario.

present with transient fever and/or a swelling around the site of

consist of dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias or oesophageal
dysmotility mimicking achalasia. Though this patient has some risk

complains of a chronic cough with night sweats for five weeks. On direct

undergoes Mantoux testing and has a 2mm area of induration. He has
never had BCG vaccination as far as he is aware and has no vaccination

BCG vaccination
HIV testing and if negative then BCG vaccination
Prophylactic anti-TB treatment
Repeat TB screening in six weeks

A 27-year-old man who recently immigrated to the UK from Ethiopia

father died from lung related problems following chronic coughs.
Following a chest X-ray and blood tests he is diagnosed with TB and
contact tracing is started. His 25-year-old male partner lives with him
and is identified as being at high risk of contracting TB. The partner
undergoes Mantoux testing and has a 2mm area of induration. He has
never had BCG vaccination as far as he is aware and has no vaccination
scar. What is the most appropriate management that should be offered
to the partner?
options: HIV testing and if negative then BCG vaccination
Repeat TB screening in six weeks
explanation:
The correct answer is HIV testing and if negative then BCG vaccination.
The low area of response to the Mantoux testing indicates that he is
unlikely to have TB and has not been vaccinated. However, the test can
be a false negative result in an immunosuppressed patient. As the
partner is at increased risk of HIV, NICE advises that an HIV test should
be done prior to vaccination. BCG vaccination is a live vaccination and
therefore is contraindicated in an immunosuppressed patient. Of note,
previous vaccination can lead to a false positive result.
NICE advises that once a diagnosis of pulmonary TB has been made
then close contacts should be managed as follow:
If asymptomatic and younger than 65 years then test for latent TB. If
Mantoux-negative and unvaccinated then offer vaccination. If at risk
of HIV then test for HIV first.
If asymptomatic and older than 65 years then assess with a chest X-
ray.
Treatment for TB should be considered if TB is confirmed and not used
prophylactically. Repeat screening is generally not used.
Source:
'Tuberculosis NICE Guidelines.' The National Institute for Health and Care
Excellence, 13 Jan. 2016.

Yellow fever is endemic around the equator mainly in Africa. It is
transmitted by the Aedes mosquitoes there. Characteristically the
patient presents with fever and constitutional symptoms. Jaundice is a
main clinical sign associated most of the times with conjunctival
injection. Other important clinical signs are relative bradycardia, and
hemorrhagic diathesis. The cause of death is due to multi-organ failure.
Blood tests generally show leucopenia with predominant neutropenia
but this is not specific. Liver enzymes are elevated most of the time.
Diagnosis depends on a high degree of suspicion for the disease and but
also more important on serology which is highly specific for this lethal
condition.
Treatment is mainly supportive.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis could present with fever and jaundice.
This would happen in the context of ascending cholangitis (fever + pain
+ jaundice) with a long history of abdominal discomfort. Liver profile
would reflect obstructive changes.
Malaria should be excluded in any patient who had traveled to an
endemic area and developed fever. The picture in our patient was not
typical and the blood film had been negative for malaria parasites.
However one has to keep it in mind if the clinical picture fits. In that case
one needs to repeat the blood film and to order serology.
Leptospirosis is a consideration here. But it usually responds to
antibiotics. Liver enzymes would generally be more mildly elevated.
Dengue fever mainly presents with headache, fever and rash. It is mainly
endemic in South East Asia.

You are the medical basic specialist trainee on call and have been asked
to see a gentleman who has just been admitted for a bad chest
infection. According to the ward nurse, he has developed an allergic
reaction after five minutes of vancomycin i.v infusion.
On arrival you proceed to examine this young man who is febrile,
obviously unwell and receiving oxygen via nasal prongs. He claims he
had not developed any new symptoms since admission but felt sudden
warmth and flushing few minutes into his vancomycin drip. On
examination he has crepitations in his left base.
Apart from generalised erythema he appears to be stable and there is no
immediate danger to his airways. His blood pressure was 105/67mmHg,
pulse was 99b/min and oxygen saturation on 4L oxygen was 95% (all
observations are similar to previous readings). He has never taken
vancomycin but states he is allergic to penicillin and ciprofloxacin.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the next step in your management?
Immediately stop vancomycin
Continue vancomycin but at a slower rate
Continue vancomycin rate unchanged
Administer i.v chlorphenamine maleate and stop vancomycin
Urgent i.m adrenaline
Question 45 of 287
You are the medical basic specialist trainee on call and have been asked
to see a gentleman who has just been admitted for a bad chest
infection. According to the ward nurse, he has developed an allergic
reaction after five minutes of vancomycin i.v infusion.
On arrival you proceed to examine this young man who is febrile,
obviously unwell and receiving oxygen via nasal prongs. He claims he
had not developed any new symptoms since admission but felt sudden
warmth and flushing few minutes into his vancomycin drip. On
examination he has crepitations in his left base.
Apart from generalised erythema he appears to be stable and there is no
immediate danger to his airways. His blood pressure was 105/67mmHg,
pulse was 99b/min and oxygen saturation on 4L oxygen was 95% (all
observations are similar to previous readings). He has never taken
vancomycin but states he is allergic to penicillin and ciprofloxacin.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the next step in your management?
options: Continue vancomycin but at a slower rate
Administer i.v chlorphenamine maleate and stop vancomycin
explanation:
Answer: continue vancomycin but at a slower rate.
This is typical red man syndrome caused by rapid infusion of
vancomycin i.v. Vancomycin should be administered diluted and at a rate
of 10mg/minutes for doses over 500mg i.v.
It is an IgE independent mast cell degranulation reaction that occurs up
to 10 minutes into receiving vancomycin i.v at a fast rate. It is not a true
allergic reaction thus vancomycin should be continued but at a lower
rate of infusion.
Antihistamine prophylaxis, lower but frequent dosing and 2 hour infusion
rate have been found to reduce the incidence of red man syndrome.
This gentleman is obviously unwell but his vitals and chest findings are
more in keeping with his chest infection and possible sepsis.

A 25-year-old sexually active woman presents with abnormal vaginal

(NAAT) for sexually transmitted infections is performed.
NAAT
positive for Chlamydia trachomatis
She has no allergies, is using oral contraceptives, and is not pregnant or
breastfeeding.
What antibiotic is most appropriate in this case?
explanation:
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance states
that doxycycline is now the first-line treatment for anyone over the age
of 13 diagnosed with Chlamydia who is not pregnant or breastfeeding.
This is therefore the correct answer.
Azithromycin is the second-line treatment recommended by NICE for
treating Chlamydia in patients for whom doxycycline is contraindicated
or not tolerated.
Chlamydia - treat with doxycycline
Ceftriaxone is used in the treatment of Gonorrhoea but is not
recommended for treating Chlamydia.
Erythromycin is a third-line agent recommended by NICE for treating
Chlamydia in patients for whom both doxycycline and azithromycin are
contraindicated or not tolerated.
Trimethoprim is indicated in treating urinary tract infections in some
populations however is not used in the treatment of Chlamydia.

A 33-year-old male with a previous history of asthma and HIV presents
for review to HIV clinic. He has been noticing weight gain, marks on his
abdomen and his partner has noticed that his face has been looking
more heavy-set over the last two months. He was diagnosed as having
HIV at the age of 19 following needle sharing and use of heroin. He has
had good retroviral control following starting treatment at the age of 20
with tenofovir, emtricitabine, atazanavir and ritonavir. His asthma has
been well controlled with only salbutamol until six months ago when due
to recurrent exacerbation due to upper respiratory tract infection his
treatment was escalated to include regular fluticasone. Repeat blood
tests show an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 900
cells/microliter. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
Weight gain secondary to tenofovir use
Weight gain secondary to emtricitabine use
Weight gain due to reduced exercise tolerance
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome
Iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome
Question 48 of 287
A 33-year-old male with a previous history of asthma and HIV presents
for review to HIV clinic. He has been noticing weight gain, marks on his
abdomen and his partner has noticed that his face has been looking
more heavy-set over the last two months. He was diagnosed as having
HIV at the age of 19 following needle sharing and use of heroin. He has
had good retroviral control following starting treatment at the age of 20
with tenofovir, emtricitabine, atazanavir and ritonavir. His asthma has
been well controlled with only salbutamol until six months ago when due
to recurrent exacerbation due to upper respiratory tract infection his
treatment was escalated to include regular fluticasone. Repeat blood
tests show an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 900
cells/microliter. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Weight gain secondary to tenofovir use
Weight gain secondary to emtricitabine use
Weight gain due to reduced exercise tolerance
explanation:
The correct answer is iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. HIV protease
inhibitors are potent P450 inhibitors. This means that there are many
possible interactions that should be checked before starting treatment.
In this gentleman, hepatic enzyme inhibition has resulted in increased
steroid dose from his regular inhaler for his asthma. This also explains
the physical description showing standard Cushingoid features.
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is possible but is less likely, and weight
gain from other causes would not explain all the physical changes
described.
Saberi, Parya, Tony Phengrasamy, and Dong Phuong Nguyen. Inhaled
Corticosteroid Use in HIV-Positive Individuals Taking Protease Inhibitors:
A Review of Pharmacokinetics, Case Reports, and Clinical Management.
HIV medicine 14.9 (2013): 519529. PMC. Web. 7 Mar. 2017.

A 22-year-old second generation British Pakistani is seen by the
Tuberculosis (TB) Specialist Nurse as part of the contact tracing service.
Her mother has recently been diagnosed with active TB after presenting
to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of night sweats, weight
loss, and haemoptysis.
The patient is clinically well and denies any focal symptomatology. Her
past medical history is unremarkable and she is a non-smoker. She
studies full-time at university but continues to live at home with her
extended family. She was fully immunised as a child.
On examination, she is afebrile. Her respiratory rate is 16/min and her
oxygen saturations are 97% breathing room air. There is no cervical
lymphadenopathy, her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft and non-
tender.
A Mantoux test is performed and read 72 hours later, at which time a
7mm area of induration is noted lying within a 16mm area of erythema.
An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is requested. What does a
positive IGRA indicate?
Latent TB or prior immunisation
Latent TB
Prior immunisation
Active or latent TB
Active TB or prior immunisation
Question 49 of 287
A 22-year-old second generation British Pakistani is seen by the
Tuberculosis (TB) Specialist Nurse as part of the contact tracing service.
Her mother has recently been diagnosed with active TB after presenting
to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of night sweats, weight
loss, and haemoptysis.
The patient is clinically well and denies any focal symptomatology. Her
past medical history is unremarkable and she is a non-smoker. She
studies full-time at university but continues to live at home with her
extended family. She was fully immunised as a child.
On examination, she is afebrile. Her respiratory rate is 16/min and her
oxygen saturations are 97% breathing room air. There is no cervical
lymphadenopathy, her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft and non-
tender.
A Mantoux test is performed and read 72 hours later, at which time a
7mm area of induration is noted lying within a 16mm area of erythema.
An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is requested. What does a
positive IGRA indicate?
explanation:
The area of induration described in the vignette constitutes a positive
Mantoux test. The area of surrounding erythema is not taken into
account.
We are told that the patient has been fully immunised as a child and she
may have therefore received the Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG)
vaccination; a cause of a falsely positive Mantoux test. The other
possibilities, in this case, are active or latent TB. An IGRA would be
advantageous in this setting as prior BCG vaccination does not produce
a false positive result. A positive test would, therefore, indicate prior
exposure to M. tuberculosis.
The main disadvantage of the IGRA is its inability to distinguish between
active and latent TB.

A 25-year-old man presents to the genitourinary medicine clinic with a
penile lesion which has been present for the last three weeks but is now
starting to reduce in size. He has had two sexual partners in the last 2
months, who were both men. There is no history of travel outside of the
UK in the last 3 years.
The lesion is a shallow ulcer with well-defined margins, which is not
tender to palpation. He has some non-tender enlarged lymph nodes on
both sides in the inguinal region.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Chancroid
Donovanosis
Lymphogranuloma venereum
M-pox
Primary syphilis
Question 50 of 287
A 25-year-old man presents to the genitourinary medicine clinic with a
penile lesion which has been present for the last three weeks but is now
starting to reduce in size. He has had two sexual partners in the last 2
months, who were both men. There is no history of travel outside of the
UK in the last 3 years.
The lesion is a shallow ulcer with well-defined margins, which is not
tender to palpation. He has some non-tender enlarged lymph nodes on
both sides in the inguinal region.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is primary syphilis , which is caused by Treponema
pallidum. This classically presents with a chancre at the site of entry of
infection. This usually starts as a painless papule, which evolves into a
painless ulcer. The lesion is usually single but multiple lesions can occur.
It generally heals over a few weeks.
Chancroid is incorrect. This is a sexually transmitted disease caused by
Haemophilus ducreyi. However, unlike in this patient, the ulcers are
Primary syphilis is associated with painless ulceration
commonly multiple and very painful. The inguinal lymphadenopathy in
chancroid is also generally painful. Chancroid is rare in the UK, and most
cases are acquired abroad in Africa or South East Asia.
Donovanosis is incorrect. This condition is also called granuloma
inguinale and is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. The genital ulcers in
this condition are painless with a classically 'beefy red' base. This
diagnosis is less likely in this patient because the ulcers would not start
to heal without treatment but would continue to enlarge, and because it
is rarely seen in the UK. It is most commonly seen in tropical regions.
Lymphogranuloma venereum is incorrect. This is caused by serovars L1,
L2 and L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis . It is more common in tropical areas
but does occur in the UK, mainly in men who have sex with men. It can
cause painless ulceration in the primary stage, but unlike in this
scenario, the ulcers are small and heal within 1-3 days so this stage is
generally not noticed by patients. The secondary stage is characterised
by painful swollen inguinal lymph nodes or anal symptoms in patients
who have acquired an anal/rectal infection.
M-pox is incorrect. The M-pox virus classically causes painful vesicular
lesions, which usually start at the site of inoculation and are generally
multiple. The lesions may then spread to involve other areas of the body.

A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with cough,
haemoptysis, and episodes of epistaxis. Additionally, she reports a two
week history of fatigue, fever and muscle aches.
On examination, she appears icteric. Coarse crackles are heard on her
chest and she has right upper quadrant tenderness. There is tenderness
in both her calves and in her lower back.
She is usually fit and well, working as a vet in a nearby town. She is a
non-smoker and consumes around 20 units of alcohol a week. At home,
she has a pet cat.
Which of the following is most appropriate for this patient?
Advise her to isolate for the course of her infection as she is at
risk of transmission to others
Advise serology testing is most likely to confirm the diagnosis
After recovery she should be offered a vaccine as she has
occupational risk
Offer a short course of oral ciprofloxacin
She should be warned that her cat was likely the source of her
infection
Question 51 of 287
A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with cough,
haemoptysis, and episodes of epistaxis. Additionally, she reports a two
week history of fatigue, fever and muscle aches.
On examination, she appears icteric. Coarse crackles are heard on her
chest and she has right upper quadrant tenderness. There is tenderness
in both her calves and in her lower back.
She is usually fit and well, working as a vet in a nearby town. She is a
non-smoker and consumes around 20 units of alcohol a week. At home,
she has a pet cat.
Which of the following is most appropriate for this patient?
options: Advise her to isolate for the course of her infection as she is at risk of transmission to others
Advise serology testing is most likely to confirm the diagnosis
After recovery she should be offered a vaccine as she has occupational risk
Offer a short course of oral ciprofloxacin
She should be warned that her cat was likely the source of her infection
explanation:
Serology is the most commonly used test for the diagnosis of
leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not be present until after 7
days
This patient has occupational and social history that increase the risk of
zoonotic infections. She has presented with a febrile illness with
components which include liver involvement and a coagulopathy.
Together with myalgia classically affecting the calves and lower back
this is suggestive of leptospirosis.
The diagnosis is most commonly made by serological testing for
specific antibodies. It is difficult to isolate the organism by culture. The
greatest diagnostic yield for culture is if it is done in the first 10 days of
the illness. After this point, the organisms are only intermittently present
in the blood. This patient has had symptoms for at least 2 weeks and
therefore culture pick-up rates are now even lower.
An infected individual will shed leptospires in their urine for the period of
the illness and for a time afterwards. Hence there is in theory a
transmittable route to others but only in a specific way. Respiratory
droplet transmission does not occur and so normal social interactions
are safe.
There is no vaccine against leptospirosis available. Therefore, hand
hygiene is important in those with occupational risk.
Most cases of leptospirosis are mild and self-resolve without
pharmacological management. Where antibiotics are employed,
doxycycline or azithromycin are often used. Amoxicillin is also effective.
Leptospirosis is classically associated with rats, which are the most
common source of transmission, but other sources include dogs, cattle
and pigs.

explanation:
This patient clearly has an infective process so much of the data
(headache, fever, myalgia, vital signs) can be discarded as being
common to all the answers.
We're now left with more concrete findings: jaundice,
hepatosplenomegaly and a raised creatinine.
Now we take one of these findings, hepatosplenomegaly and consider
the differential diagnosis:
Causes of hepatosplenomegaly
chronic liver disease with portal hypertension
infections: glandular fever, malaria, hepatitis
lymphoproliferative disorders
myeloproliferative disorders e.g. chronic myeloid leukaemia
amyloidosis
This suggests that malaria is the most likely diagnosis. Jaundice and a
raised creatinine are consistent with this.

What is the most appropriate management option?
explanation:
The patient has PCP pneumonia, caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii - a
yeast-like fungus which is an opportunistic pathogen. The treatment for
this is co-trimoxazole.
Pneumocystis jiroveci penumonia is treated with co-trimoxazole,
which is a mix of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole
All patients with dermatomyositis or polymyositis with pulmonary
fibrosis who are treated with glucocorticoids are advised to receive PCP
prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole. Stopping steroids would not be
appropriate in this scenario.
It is important to note that not all patients taking glucocorticoids for
rheumatological conditions require PCP prophylaxis. However, there is
evidence that in non-HIV cohorts, the greatest risk for developing PCP is
glucocorticoid use and deficiencies in innate and acquired immune
components. Therefore, although there are currently no formal
guidelines it is recommended that if an individual satisfies both these
criteria in rheumatological conditions, they should be considered for PCP
prophylaxis.
For example the following all should be considered for prophylaxis:
A patient on the equivalent of 20 mg prednisolone or greater for one
month plus the concomitant use of another immunosuppressive
drug
Dermatomyositis on high dose prednisolone for greater than one
month and pulmonary fibrosis
Allogenic or autogenic stem cell transplant or solid organ
transplantation

explanation:
The most likely explanation for the patient's condition is a drug reaction
called red man syndrome secondary to vancomycin infusion. This is not
an allergic reaction as demonstrated by the lack of cardiorespiratory
distress, subcutaneous oedema, wheals or urticaria. The reaction is
more of a rate dependent infusion reaction. Treatment involves slowing
down the infusion of vancomycin and administration of anti-histamines.

Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic used in the treatment of Gram-

inhibits cell wall formation by binding to D-Ala-D-Ala moieties,

alteration to the terminal amino acid residues of the NAM/NAG-
