A 41-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus
presents with a nodular lesion on the right-side of his face around the
angle of the jaw. One month ago he had a tooth extraction at the dentist.
The nodule is around 2 cm in diameter, raised and purple-red in colour.
On examination a sinus tract is seen in the middle of the nodule which is
draining a blood-stained fluid.
Microscopy of the discharge shows microscopic yellow granules.
What is the most likely causative organism?
Actinomyces israelii
Tunga penetrans
Klebsiella
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Escherichia coli
Question 122 of 287
A 41-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus
presents with a nodular lesion on the right-side of his face around the
angle of the jaw. One month ago he had a tooth extraction at the dentist.
The nodule is around 2 cm in diameter, raised and purple-red in colour.
On examination a sinus tract is seen in the middle of the nodule which is
draining a blood-stained fluid.
Microscopy of the discharge shows microscopic yellow granules.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is Actinomyces israelii. The patient's presentation of
a nodular lesion with a sinus tract draining blood-stained fluid and the
presence of microscopic yellow granules in the discharge are
characteristic features of actinomycosis, which is most commonly
caused by Actinomyces israelii. Actinomycosis is an indolent, slowly
progressive infection that often occurs following dental procedures or
oral trauma. The presence of microscopic yellow granules, also known
as 'sulfur granules,' further supports this diagnosis.
Tunga penetrans, also known as the chigoe flea, causes tungiasis, which
typically presents with pruritic papules or nodules on the feet. This
clinical presentation does not match the patient's facial lesion and
history of tooth extraction.
Klebsiella species are gram-negative bacteria that can cause a variety of
infections, including pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and soft tissue
infections. However, these infections do not typically present with
nodular lesions and sinus tracts containing sulfur granules.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is another gram-negative bacterium that can
cause various infections such as skin and soft tissue infections,
particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Although Pseudomonas
aeruginosa can cause skin lesions, it does not produce sulfur granules
nor form sinus tracts like those seen in actinomycosis.
Finally, Escherichia coli is a gram-negative bacterium commonly
associated with gastrointestinal and urinary tract infections. It can
occasionally cause skin and soft tissue infections but would not present
with the characteristic nodular lesion containing sulfur granules seen in
this patient.

A 75-year-old male with a long history of intravenous drug use is
admitted with fevers, rigors and back pain. Three sets of blood cultures
taken at admission grow positive for gram positive cocci in clusters. He
is suspected of having Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and is
commenced on intravenous vancomycin.
Half an hour after the infusion is commenced, he is noted by the nurse to
be flushed. On examination, he is noted to have erythema over his neck,
face and trunk but denies any significant distress or discomfort.
His observations are as follow: blood pressure 125/70 mmHg, heart rate
85/min, temperature of 36.8ºC, respiratory rate of 18/min and oxygen
saturation of 98% on room air.
Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
Stopping the vancomycin infusion, administering 200mg of IV
hydrocortisone and informing the patient that he is allergic to the
medication
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and administering a single
dose of 0.5mcg intramuscular adrenaline
Stopping the vancomycin infusion until symptoms resolve and
then re-starting a slower rate
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and prescribing topical 1%
hydrocortisone cream to affected areas
Continuing the vancomycin infusion and administering 1000 ml
of 0.9% saline solution over 1 hour

face and trunk but denies any significant distress or discomfort.
His observations are as follow: blood pressure 125/70 mmHg, heart rate
85/min, temperature of 36.8ºC, respiratory rate of 18/min and oxygen
saturation of 98% on room air.
Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Stopping the vancomycin infusion, administering 200mg of IV hydrocortisone and informing the patient that he is allergic to the medication
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and administering a single dose of 0.5mcg intramuscular adrenaline
Stopping the vancomycin infusion until symptoms resolve and then re-starting a slower rate
Stopping the vancomycin infusion and prescribing topical 1% hydrocortisone cream to affected areas
Continuing the vancomycin infusion and administering 1000 ml of 0.9% saline solution over 1 hour
explanation:
Red man syndrome is associated with rapid intravenous infusion
vancomycin. It is a common adverse reaction of intravenous vancomycin
use and is a distinct entity from anaphylaxis due to vancomycin use.
Typical symptoms include redness, pruritus and a burning sensation,
predominantly in the upper body (face, neck and upper chest). Severe
cases can be associated with hypotension and chest pain.
The pathophysiology of red man syndrome is attributed to vancomycin-
related activation of mast cells with release of histamine.
The management of red man syndrome involves cessation of the
infusion, and when symptoms have resolved, recommencement at a
slower rate. In patients who are more symptomatic antihistamines can
be administered, and may require intravenous fluids if the syndrome is
associated with hypotension.
References:
Sivagnanam S, Deleu D, Red man syndrome. Crit Care. 2003
Apr;7(2):119-20
Bruneira FR, Ferreira FM, Saviolli LR, Bacci MR, Feder D, et al. The
use of vancomycin with its therapeutic and adverse effects: a review
Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci. 2015 Feb;19(4):694-700.

A 34-year-old man is referred to the medical admissions unit with joint
pain and swelling in his hands and feet. One month prior to his
attendance, he had developed an illness while travelling in Colombia,
which was characterized by fever, headache, rash and debilitating
polyarthralgia. His treating physicians noted mild hepatomegaly at the
time. He recovered well from this episode without intervention, except
for his ongoing musculoskeletal symptoms.
Examination reveals a small joint polyarthritis of the hands and feet.
Abdominal examination was unremarkable.
Serological testing is positive for an RNA virus.
What is the likely diagnosis?
Chikungunya virus
Dengue
Epstein Barr Virus (EBV)
Parvovirus
Zika virus
Question 127 of 287
A 34-year-old man is referred to the medical admissions unit with joint
pain and swelling in his hands and feet. One month prior to his
attendance, he had developed an illness while travelling in Colombia,
which was characterized by fever, headache, rash and debilitating
polyarthralgia. His treating physicians noted mild hepatomegaly at the
time. He recovered well from this episode without intervention, except
for his ongoing musculoskeletal symptoms.
Examination reveals a small joint polyarthritis of the hands and feet.
Abdominal examination was unremarkable.
Serological testing is positive for an RNA virus.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chikungunya is the correct answer. This is an RNA alpha-virus
characterized by sudden onset fever accompanied by skin rashes and
joint pain followed by persistent rheumatic symptoms. In contrast to the
other diagnoses, which can all cause headache, fever and rash, the
polyarthralgia is said to be far more debilitating and it is most
Chikungunya can present with debilitating joint pain
associated with the development of persistent musculoskeletal
symptoms. Furthermore, hepatomegaly can be a feature of this
condition but this is not seen in Zika or dengue. While hepatomegaly is a
feature of EBV, this is a DNA virus and is less likely to cause persistent
musculoskeletal symptoms.
Zika virus is characterized by a pruritic maculopapular rash
accompanied by other symptoms such as fever, headache, conjunctivitis,
myalgia and arthralgia. It is an RNA virus but is much less likely to cause
persistent musculoskeletal symptoms.
Dengue is incorrect. This is another RNA arbovirus that causes fever,
rash and arthralgia in addition to other features such as
thrombocytopenia. However, hepatomegaly is not a feature and it is not
associated with the development of persistent arthritis.
Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) is incorrect. This is a DNA virus.
Musculoskeletal manifestations are less prominent.
Parvovirus is incorrect. This can cause rash, hepatomegaly and
polyarthritis but it is a DNA virus.

explanation:
Leptospirosis is caused by zoonotic spirochete bacteria, spread via
contact with infected animal urine. Animals such as rodents act as
reservoirs of infection, shedding the bacteria in their urine which
subsequently enter mucous membranes and broken skin. Freshwater
swimming and other watersports are associated with leptospirosis
infection. After an incubation period of 7 - 14 days, the disease presents
in a biphasic fashion: acute fever, malaise, headache, and abdominal
pain followed by severe systemic upset such as renal failure, pulmonary
haemorrhage, and hepatic failure. Thrombocytopenia is also seen
(suggested mechanisms include poor production by bone marrow and
immune-mediated platelet destruction). Serology is the most commonly
used test for the diagnosis of leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not
be present until after 7 days.
Serology is the most commonly used test for the diagnosis of
leptospirosis, however, antibodies may not be present until after 7
days
Leishmania brasiliensis is the unicellular parasite responsible for
cutaneous and mucosal leishmaniasis. Endemic in South America, this
disease presents with skin and mucosal ulcerative lesions and is spread
by the sandfly. Leishmaniasis is diagnosed by detecting Leishmania
parasites (or DNA) in tissue specimens. This patient had no such skin
lesions and no history of insect bites.
This patient's hepatitis serology demonstrates that she has been
exposed to hepatitis B (positive anti-HBc and anti-HBs) but has cleared
the virus (negative HBsAg). Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) is an indicator
of viral replication and correlates with hepatitis B virus infectivity. This
would typically be measured if the patient had active hepatitis B. As this
patient is HepBsAg negative, this test is not necessary.
Schistosoma haematobium is a parasitic fluke endemic to areas of
Africa. The intermediate host is the freshwater snail; transmission risk is
increased by swimming in such bodies of water. Whilst acute infection
can cause a transient febrile illness (Katayama syndrome) the history
typically includes pruritis (swimmers itch) with eosinophilia.
Schistosomiasis is primarily a chronic disease with Schistosoma
haematobium causing urological manifestations such as cystitis or
obstructive uropathy. Examination of the urine for ova is the primary
method used to diagnose suspected Schistosoma haematobium
infections.
Treponema pallidum a sexually transmitted bacterial spirochete
responsible for causing syphilis. Primary syphilis is characterised by a
painless self-limiting genital ulcer (chancre) and lymphadenopathy
occurring 10-90 days after sexual transmission. Secondary syphilis
occurs following the haematogenous spread of the bacteria and can
present with a variety of symptoms including a widespread rash,
adenopathy, arthralgia, hepatitis, and alopecia. This classically presents
4-8 weeks after the presentation of the chancre. Whilst this diagnosis
should be considered given the patient's sexual history, there is no
mention of a genital lesion in the question stem, and the very short
period between the sexual encounter (8 days prior) and the onset of her
symptoms is not typical of secondary syphilis. The Treponema pallidum
particle agglutination (TPPA) assay is one of many tests that may be
used to detect specific anti-treponemal antibodies in serum. This is
usually only requested after a positive non-treponemal screening test in
the diagnostic workup of syphilis.

What is the most appropriate treatment?
Immunoglobulin

immunoglobulin
Measles-only vaccine

Question 130 of 287
A 46-year-old man telephones his GP for advice. Five days ago, he was in
contact with his nephew, who was unwell and had a rash at the time. It
has since been confirmed that his nephew has measles. The patient is
concerned as he was not immunised against measles as a child.
Furthermore, he takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis.
He has no symptoms currently.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and immunoglobulin
explanation:
The most appropriate course of action, for a patient who is
immunosuppressed and does not have adequate immunity to measles,
is to administer immunoglobulin following exposure. Ideally, this should
be done within 72 hours, but can be done up until 6 days post-exposure.
For patients with normal immunity, who have not been fully immunised
against measles, the MMR vaccine should be administered within 72
hours of exposure.
Those exposed to measles can be given immunoglobulin to reduce
the risk of infection
Administering both the MMR vaccine and immunoglobulin is
inappropriate. This can invalidate the effect of the vaccine.
Giving the measles-only vaccine would also be inappropriate. This
patient should be given immunoglobulin. For a patient with normal
immunity, who is not fully immunised, the MMR vaccine should be given
rather than a measles-only vaccine.
No treatment is incorrect. Given this patient's clear exposure and history
of both immunosuppression and lack of immunisation against measles,
immunoglobulin should be given.

A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
shortness of breath, fever and a cough. He has had a non-productive
cough for two weeks. Before this, he had felt unwell with muscle aches
and malaise. He went to his GP and was given amoxicillin but this has
made no difference and now he is feeling more breathless and unwell.
He has not been outside of the UK in the last year. He has no other
medical problems and takes no regular medications. His cough is non-
productive and comes in paroxysms which make him concerned.
On examination, there are a few bilateral crepitations, but the
examination is otherwise normal. His observations show fever and mild
hypoxia. Blood tests show mild anaemia and raised inflammatory
markers. A chest X-ray shows bilateral consolidation, but he improves
with IV co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin over a few days.
What is the most likely causative organism?
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Legionella pneumophila
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Chlamydia psittaci
Coxiella burnetii
Question 133 of 287
A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
shortness of breath, fever and a cough. He has had a non-productive
cough for two weeks. Before this, he had felt unwell with muscle aches
and malaise. He went to his GP and was given amoxicillin but this has
made no difference and now he is feeling more breathless and unwell.
He has not been outside of the UK in the last year. He has no other
medical problems and takes no regular medications. His cough is non-
productive and comes in paroxysms which make him concerned.
On examination, there are a few bilateral crepitations, but the
examination is otherwise normal. His observations show fever and mild
hypoxia. Blood tests show mild anaemia and raised inflammatory
markers. A chest X-ray shows bilateral consolidation, but he improves
with IV co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin over a few days.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The correct answer is Mycoplasma pneumoniae. There are several hints
in this history and investigations to suggest Mycoplasma pneumoniae
as the likely cause. First of all, he is a young and fit patient who
describes a non-productive cough preceded by flu-like symptoms and
not responding to penicillins. Secondly, he has anaemia which may be
due to haemolysis, and finally there is bilateral consolidation on the
chest X-ray. Klebsiella pneumoniae is more typical in alcoholics,
Legionella pneumophila is associated with a history of foreign travel,
Chlamydia psittaci is associated with contact and exposure to birds and
finally, Coxiella burnetii is rare and associated with farm animal
exposure.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a cause of atypical pneumonia that often
affects younger patients. It is associated with a number of characteristic
complications such as erythema multiforme and cold autoimmune
haemolytic anaemia. Epidemics of Mycoplasma pneumoniae classically
occur every 4 years. It is important to recognise atypical pneumonia as it
may not respond to penicillins or cephalosporins due to it lacking a
peptidoglycan cell wall.

his GP as he presented with dysuria and a negative urine dipstick test. A
sexual health screen, including blood tests for HIV and syphilis serology,
are requested. What form of consent is required?
options: Written consent for HIV testing and verbal consent for sexual health screening
explanation:
The correct answer is verbal consent. Consent clearly is needed as an
investigation is done but since syphilis and HIV are transmittable
diseases consent needs to be specific towards each. This means that
the patient must be aware that they are being tested for HIV and syphilis
rather than just aware that they are having a routine blood test. Written
consent is not needed, and may discourage patients from having testing.
Source:
UK National Guidelines for HIV Testing 2008. London: British HIV
Association, 2008
(see page 10)

explanation:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a herpes virus which commonly leads to
infectious mononucleosis. This presents, often in teenagers and young
adults with fevers, painful throat, lymphadenopathy and flu-like
symptoms. Although it can last longer the symptoms are usually self-
limiting within 2 weeks. Acute infection often leads to splenomegaly or
hepatosplenomegaly and although a transient hepatitis is common it
can lead to clinical jaundice.
Infectious mononucleosis
Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is caused by the Epstein-Barr
virus (EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, HHV-4) in 90% of cases.
Less frequent causes include cytomegalovirus and HHV-6. It is most
common in adolescents and young adults.
The classic triad of sore throat, pyrexia and lymphadenopathy is seen in
around 98% of patients:
sore throat
lymphadenopathy: may be present in the anterior and posterior
triangles of the neck, in contrast to tonsillitis which typically only
results in the upper anterior cervical chain being enlarged
pyrexia
Other features include:
malaise, anorexia, headache
palatal petechiae
splenomegaly - occurs in around 50% of patients and may rarely
predispose to splenic rupture
hepatitis, transient rise in ALT
lymphocytosis: presence of 50% lymphocytes with at least 10%
atypical lymphocytes
haemolytic anaemia secondary to cold agglutins (IgM)
a maculopapular, pruritic rash develops in around 99% of patients
who take ampicillin/amoxicillin whilst they have infectious
mononucleosis
Symptoms typically resolve after 2-4 weeks.

Question 137 of 287
A 69-year-old woman with diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis presents to
the clinic complaining of malaise. She takes metformin, sulfasalazine
and hydroxychloroquine daily and methotrexate once a week. She
volunteers at a care home near her home. On examination, she appears
frail, and her fingers and toes are deformed. She is alert, afebrile and
comfortable at rest. Her pulse rate is 70 beats per minute, BP is 120/80
mmHg, and respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute. On inspection of
her legs, you notice the following:
© Image used on license from DermNet NZ
What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this
patient?
options: Admit and treat with intravenous antibiotics
Order for an x-ray of the limb
Order for blood cultures and review with reports after one week
Prescribe oral antibiotics and arrange a follow-up visit for the next week
Prescribe oral prednisolone and arrange a follow-up visit
explanation:
The most appropriate next step is to admit and treat with intravenous
antibiotics. The image provided shows a swollen and erythematous right
lower limb. Differential diagnoses for a swollen limb include cellulitis,
deep vein thrombosis (DVT), lymphoedema, and fluid overload
conditions such as chronic heart failure. Cellulitis should be suspected
when there is a history of fever and malaise, with superficial bullae
potentially observed over the affected area. DVT typically presents in
patients who have risk factors (such as recent immobilisation, surgery,
or pregnancy) with unilateral limb oedema, erythema, and tenderness.
Lymphoedema often has an insidious onset and manifests as a slowly
progressive swelling of a limb; it is commonly observed in patients post-
lymph node dissection proximal to the affected area. Fluid overload
states usually present with bilateral pitting pedal oedema without
associated warmth or tenderness.
In this case, we are presented with a frail, immunocompromised woman
exhibiting symptoms of right leg cellulitis. These characteristics'frailty
and an immunocompromised state'are indications for in-patient
management according to NICE guidelines on admission criteria for
cellulitis. It is important to note that methotrexate is typically withheld
for patients who are being hospitalized with severe infections requiring
intravenous antibiotic therapy.
Ordering an x-ray of the limb is not correct. While cellulitis is diagnosed
clinically, an x-ray may be warranted only if there is strong clinical
suspicion of osteomyelitis in the underlying bone; otherwise, it does not
play a role in the management of cellulitis itself. Ultrasound (USG),
computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can
help exclude deeper tissue infections such as myositis or detect
abscess formation.
Ordering blood cultures and reviewing after one week is inappropriate
for this scenario. This patient has an acute infection necessitating
immediate antibiotic treatment. Blood cultures are indicated when
sepsis is suspected but should not delay empirical antibiotic therapy
aimed at preventing infection progression.
Prescribing oral antibiotics and arranging follow-up is incorrect for this
patient's presentation. Given her frailty and immunocompromised status,
she requires hospital admission for intravenous antibiotic therapy rather
than outpatient management with oral antibiotics, which are reserved for
Eron class I and II cases of cellulitis.
Prescribing oral prednisolone would be ill-advised here as it could
exacerbate the infection by suppressing the immune response instead
of treating it. Prednisolone may be indicated in patients experiencing
acute rheumatoid arthritis flares but is not applicable to this clinical
situation.

Question 138 of 287
A 46-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a
history of dyspnoea, rhinorrhoea, and cough. She reports a low-grade
fever and general malaise. On systemic examination, the only notable
finding is an itchy vesicular rash distributed over her trunk. She takes no
regular medications and has no recent travel history. No constitutional
symptoms are noted.
Her vital signs are as follows: temperature 38.0°C, blood pressure
128/86 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation at
95% on room air.
A chest x-ray has been performed as part of her evaluation, shown
below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the underlying infection responsible for her condition?
explanation:
The chest radiograph reveals diffuse interstitial infiltrates scattered
throughout both lung fields, but predominantly located at the hila. There
is no sign of consolidation, which helps exclude other differentials.
Pneumonia can be a long-term complication of varicella infection as
chickenpox is transmitted via droplets. The presence of an itchy
vesicular rash should prompt consideration of varicella infection.
Varicella pneumonia typically develops 1-6 days after the onset of
cutaneous symptoms. While shingles exhibit a dermatomal distribution,
chickenpox is not restricted to dermatomes.
Aspergillosis typically affects immunocompromised individuals,
including those who are post-transplant or on immunosuppressive
therapy. In such cases, the chest X-ray might show widespread
pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation. However, aspergillosis
does not present with a vesicular rash.
Miliary tuberculosis (TB) could present with similar radiographic
findings; however, this would usually be accompanied by a history of
travel to TB-endemic regions or close contact with an individual
diagnosed with TB—none of which are evident here. Constitutional
symptoms are also associated with TB but are absent in this scenario.
Moreover, miliary TB does not manifest with a vesicular rash.
Renal cell carcinoma may lead to 'cannonball' metastases visible on
chest X-rays as large, well-circumscribed nodules within bilateral lung
fields, which differs from the diffuse calcifications observed here.
Patients may also have relevant medical or family history and typically
exhibit constitutional symptoms.
Sarcoidosis-associated rashes include lupus pernio or erythema
nodosum but do not have a vesicular character. This clinical feature
allows differentiation between sarcoidosis and varicella infections.

This is Efavirenz toxicity.
Rifampicin causes potent enzyme induction and therefore dramatically

logical.
Efavirenz however can cause neuropsychiatric toxicity (due to variable
metabolism which is genetically determined) which is the cause of
psychosis here. Normal LP excludes TB meningitis. Ethambutol causes
optic neuritis, so monitoring of visual acuity during treatment is
essential. HIV encephalopathy is possible but unlikely to present so
acutely and the temporal relation to Efavirenz introduction, in this case,
is the key.

explanation:
The candidate should have no difficulty in recognising that this patient
has meningitis. However, good knowledge of the epidemiology of
meningitis is required to answer the question completely.
The most common cause of meningitis in Saudi Arabia during Hajj is
meningococcal meningitis type A. It is also the leading cause of
epidemics of what is known as the meningitis belt in Africa along the
equator line including Sudan, Ethiopia and Nigeria.
Type B and Type C are mainly responsible for sporadic cases of
meningitis in Europe and South America.

He smokes 10 cigarettes a day, drinks approximately 30 units of alcohol

His Glasgow Coma Score is 15/15. Neurological examination reveals

supinator reflexes are absent. Knee and ankle reflexes are normal. His
pupils are dilated and sluggish in reaction to light. He is unable to abduct
either eye. You notice needle track marks on the patient's forearm and an
erythematous wound in the patient's right antecubital fossa.
What is treatment would you give to the patient immediately?
explanation:
This patient has presented with typical features of botulism, which is
likely to have been contracted via the patient's wound in this case. He
has suffered from a descending weakness, initially affecting his bulbar
and pharyngeal muscles, then his upper limbs. If untreated this would
progress to involve his respiratory muscles and lower limbs. In contrast,
Guillain Barre Syndrome (GBS) presents with an ascending weakness
usually involving the lower limbs, then upper limbs then cranial nerves.
Both conditions show autonomic features and progress rapidly.
One particularly distressing feature of botulism is that it does not affect
GCS.
The immediate treatment of choice would be IV Trivalent antitoxin
immediately and general supportive measures.

A 24-year-old man attends the sexual health clinic complaining of
urethral discharge and dysuria following an episode of unprotected
intercourse. Examination of the external genitalia confirms purulent
discharge but no other abnormalities. There is no previous history of
sexually transmitted infection.
You undertake microscopy of the discharge which reveals many white
blood cells but no organisms. A urine sample is sent for nucleic acid
amplification tests (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria
gonorrhoea. You treat him empirically with a course of doxycycline for
presumed chlamydial infection.
He returns for review a week later. You note both NAAT results to be
negative. However, the patient tells you his symptoms have fully
resolved.
What is the most likely explanation?
Mycoplasma genitalium infection
False negative NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis
False negative NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoea
Herpes simplex virus infection
Urinary tract infection

A 24-year-old man attends the sexual health clinic complaining of
urethral discharge and dysuria following an episode of unprotected
intercourse. Examination of the external genitalia confirms purulent
discharge but no other abnormalities. There is no previous history of
sexually transmitted infection.
You undertake microscopy of the discharge which reveals many white
blood cells but no organisms. A urine sample is sent for nucleic acid
amplification tests (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria
gonorrhoea. You treat him empirically with a course of doxycycline for
presumed chlamydial infection.
He returns for review a week later. You note both NAAT results to be
negative. However, the patient tells you his symptoms have fully
resolved.
What is the most likely explanation?
options: False negative NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis
False negative NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoea
explanation:
Urethritis in a male, negative for Gonorrhoea and Chlamydia →?
Mycoplasma genitalium
The correct answer is Mycoplasma genitalium infection. This has
emerged as the leading cause of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU).
Urethritis is evidenced in this case by the symptoms of dysuria and
discharge combined with the presence of white cells in the discharge.
NGU is diagnosed when features of urethritis exist in the absence of a
positive test for gonorrhoea. Other explanations include infection with
Chlamydia or organisms such as Ureaplasma urealyticum.
False negative NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis is incorrect. Although
improvement with doxycycline would fit with Chlamydia, the sensitivity of
NAATs reaches 97% in some studies, making this a less likely
explanation.
False negative NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoea is incorrect. The
sensitivity of NAATs for gonorrhoea reaches 98-99% in some studies. We
would also not expect a symptomatic improvement with doxycycline.
Herpes simplex virus infection is incorrect. HSV most commonly
presents with painful genital ulceration. Less commonly, patients may
present with dysuria and discharge in the absence of visible ulceration.
However, we are told this patient has had no previous STIs. The first
episode of genital HSV is often severe and prolonged in the absence of
anti-viral treatment and the spontaneous improvement in 7 days
described here would be unusual. Subsequent recurrences are often less
severe and more short-lived.
Urinary tract infection is incorrect. Urinary tract infection frequently
causes dysuria but urethral discharge would be an unusual feature. It is
also very unusual to see urinary tract infections in young males in the
absence of a structural abnormality of the urinary tract or an iatrogenic
cause such as catheterisation.
Non-gonococcal urethritis

Which antibiotic was she likely to have been treated with?
explanation:
The correct answer is Trimethoprim. This is evidenced by the rise in
serum potassium from 3.7 mmol/L to 5.2 mmol/L over two days of
treatment. Trimethoprim is known to cause hyperkalaemia through its
action on the distal tubule of the kidney where it blocks the sodium
channel ENaC, leading to reduced potassium excretion. This effect is
particularly notable in elderly patients and those with reduced renal
function. The patient's other blood results show an appropriate response
to antibiotic therapy with falling WBC and CRP.
Erythromycin is not a first-line treatment for urinary tract infections in
the UK according to NICE guidelines. While it can cause various side
effects, significant changes in potassium levels are not typically
associated with its use. Additionally, it has poor urinary penetration
making it an unsuitable choice for UTIs.
Co-amoxiclav, while commonly used for UTIs, does not typically cause
hyperkalaemia. The blood results show improving inflammatory markers
which could be consistent with co-amoxiclav use, but the marked rise in
potassium would not be expected with this antibiotic.
Nitrofurantoin is a common first-line treatment for uncomplicated UTIs,
but it would be contraindicated in this patient due to her reduced renal
function (eGFR likely <45 ml/min based on her age and creatinine).
Furthermore, nitrofurantoin does not typically cause electrolyte
disturbances.
Ciprofloxacin, while effective against urinary pathogens, does not cause
significant changes in potassium levels. While it could effectively treat
this infection, the characteristic rise in potassium seen in this case
would not be expected with ciprofloxacin therapy.

explanation:
Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome occurs in immunosuppressed
individuals with coexistent Strongyloides stercoralis infection.
Uncontrolled proliferation of larvae occurs with dissemination to end
organs.
As in this individual, systemic sepsis often occurs due to involvement of
the gut wall allowing translocation of gut bacteria. Other features include
pulmonary infiltrates, paralytic ileus, gastrointestinal bleeding and
syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion.
Filariform larvae can be found in body fluids by microscopy and it is this
that confirms the diagnosis in this case. Due to immunosuppression,
eosinophilia is often absent. Given the patient's country of origin,
strongyloidosis is most likely to have been chronic, but could have been
acquired on his recent trip to Africa.
Plasmodium falciparum infection can cause a similar presentation,
although the normal blood film in this case makes this unlikely. Severe
tuberculosis infection tends to predominantly involve the lungs with a
varying degree of involvement of other organ systems.
Churg-Strauss vasculitis can cause severe abdominal symptoms
including infarction and perforation. However, the normal eosinophil
count, short history and immunosuppresion do not support this
diagnosis.
Colonic carcinoma can lead to translocation of gut bacteria and gram-
negative sepsis. However, this diagnosis would not explain all of the
findings in this case and is not supported by the normal mean cell
volume.
Strongyloides stercoralis
Strongyloides stercoralis is a human parasitic nematode worm. The
larvae are present in soil and gain access to the body by penetrating the
skin. Infection with Strongyloides stercoralis causes strongyloidiasis.

and disseminated rash. She had not been previously vaccinated and was
in contact with her 2-year-old cousin who had developed a fever and
disseminated blisters and vesicles containing clear fluid. She began to
have a fever and flu-like symptoms 2 weeks after seeing her cousin.
Similar clear-fluid filled vesicles and blisters developed 3 days later and
she was admitted for further observation.
After 3 days, she noticed that while most of her skin lesions are healing,
one of the lesions on the thigh appears to be red and becoming hot to
touch. An area of skin approximately 3x3cm was erythematous. The skin
was marked and she was commenced on IV flucloxacillin. Over the
coming 12 hours, the erythema around this lesion continued to spread.
The pain around her leg increased in intensity, requiring morphine to take
the edge off the pain. A blueish discolouration begins to develop around
the rash.
Given the likely complication that has developed, what is the likely

Given the likely complication that has developed, what is the likely

explanation:
Chickenpox is a risk factor for invasive group A streptococcal soft
tissue infections including necrotizing fasciitis
The development of fevers along with blisters and vesicles raises the
suspicion that this is caused by chickenpox. Besides, this is more likely
as she has been exposed to a child who has had similar symptoms.
Chickenpox tends to be milder in children but can cause significant
morbidity in adults.
The development of a rapidly evolving rash along with significant pains
out of proportion to the rash seen should always raise alarm bells for
necrotising fasciitis. Blueish discolouration of the skin is also suggestive
of this. A surgical review should be sought immediately.
Invasive group A Streptococcus, a β-haemolytic Streptococcus, has been
implicated as the cause for necrotizing fasciitis in patients with
chickenpox. Extremely broad-spectrum antibiotics are initially used with
the choices tailored to bacterial sensitivities when known.
Staphylococcus aureus can also result in necrotising fasciitis but is more
commonly associated with patients who have other underlying medical
conditions like diabetes.
Enterococcus faecalis does not tend to cause skin infections and are
often associated with infections like endocarditis.
Streptococcus bovis is a gamma-haemolytic Streptococcus is most often
associated with colorectal cancer associated endocarditis. It is not
associated with skin infections.
Clostridium perfringens can cause necrotising fasciitis and presents as
gas gangrene. This will present with crepitus under the skin which is not
seen here.

explanation:
The MRI scan demonstrates a large multilobulated mass in the right
frontal lobe. It homogeneously enhances and extends to involve the
caudate and the periventricular area. There is also a significant mass
effect. These findings in addition to the history are highly suggestive of
primary CNS lymphoma. The most appropriate initial treatment is
steroids (which should reduce tumour size and hence mass effect) and
methotrexate. Other future options include whole brain irradiation and
surgery.
You would not expect the enhancement to be homogenous with
toxoplasmosis, it is usually in a ring pattern.

recently spent three months in Jamaica on a beach-side yoga retreat. He
only drank bottled water and ate well cooked vegetarian food. He
ensured that any raw vegetables were peeled. He returned home three
weeks ago.
During his final week in Jamaica he noticed an itchy spot develop on the
side of his ankle. The rash has gradually spread from the original spot
slowly 'like a snake up the side of his foot'. The lesion is currently 11cm
long and is a raised itchy serpiginous linear lesion.
He is otherwise well.
What is the causative organism?
Strongyloides stercoralis
Ancylostoma braziliense

Ascaris lumbricoides

A 37 year old Caucasian male attends an outpatient clinic. He had
recently spent three months in Jamaica on a beach-side yoga retreat. He
only drank bottled water and ate well cooked vegetarian food. He
ensured that any raw vegetables were peeled. He returned home three
weeks ago.
During his final week in Jamaica he noticed an itchy spot develop on the
side of his ankle. The rash has gradually spread from the original spot
slowly 'like a snake up the side of his foot'. The lesion is currently 11cm
long and is a raised itchy serpiginous linear lesion.
He is otherwise well.
What is the causative organism?
explanation:
The correct answer in this case is Ancylostoma braziliense. The patient's
presentation of a raised, itchy serpiginous linear lesion that has
gradually spread 'like a snake' up the side of his foot is characteristic of
cutaneous larva migrans (CLM), also known as creeping eruption. CLM
is caused by the larval form of hookworms, most commonly
Ancylostoma braziliense, which are found in tropical and subtropical
regions such as Jamaica. The larvae penetrate the skin, usually through
contact with contaminated soil or sand, and migrate within the
epidermis, causing an intensely pruritic inflammatory reaction.
Strongyloides stercoralis is an incorrect option because this nematode
causes strongyloidiasis, which typically presents with gastrointestinal
symptoms such as abdominal pain and diarrhea. Skin involvement in
strongyloidiasis can occur but usually manifests as pruritic papules or
urticaria rather than the serpiginous linear lesion seen in this case.
Necator americanus is another species of hookworm, but it primarily
causes human infection through intestinal penetration rather than
cutaneous manifestations like CLM. Infection with Necator americanus
can lead to iron-deficiency anemia due to blood loss from attachment
sites in the small intestine.
Ascaris lumbricoides is a roundworm that causes ascariasis, one of the
most common helminthic infections worldwide. Ascariasis typically
presents with gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain and
bloating; however, during the larval migration phase through the lungs,
patients may experience coughing and wheezing. Cutaneous
manifestations are not typical in ascariasis.
Schistosomiasis mansoni is a blood fluke that causes schistosomiasis,
which is characterized by granulomatous inflammation in response to
the eggs of the parasite. The primary manifestation of schistosomiasis
is hepatosplenic involvement, with symptoms such as abdominal pain
and hepatomegaly. Cutaneous manifestations can occur during the
cercarial penetration phase (swimmer's itch), but this is typically a
localized pruritic papular rash rather than the serpiginous linear lesion
seen in this case.

A 23-year-old man attends the emergency department after arriving back
in the UK from a one-year trip travelling in South America. He denies any
acute medical problems but reports that he is concerned about a dog
bite he had received in Brazil about three months previously. The patient
had been on a rain-forest expedition when a dog from the village he was
staying in became aggressive and bit him on the left hand, leaving a
open wound. The local inhabitants of the village had then chased the
dog away. The patient had received first aid from his tour guide and been
provided with a course of oral antibiotics. The wound had then healed
over the following two weeks. It was only when the patient had been
speaking with fellow travellers shortly before he returned to the UK did
he realise the possible risk for rabies exposure.
The patient was well in himself and denied any neurological or other
symptoms. He had no significant past medical history and took no
regular medications. He admitted that he had no adequately researched
his travel health needs before leaving the UK and so had not had any
vaccinations prior to his trip.
Examination of the patients wound demonstrated fully healed scars
consistent with a bite marks across the palm and dorsal surface of the
wrist. The limb had normal neurological and vascular examination and
the patient reported normal function of the hand.
What is the correct statement regarding rabies post-exposure
prophylaxis for this patient?
The patient should receive rabies vaccination but not rabies
immunoglobulin as his wound has now healed
The patient does not require post-exposure prophylaxis as he
remains free of symptoms following the incubation period of rabies
The patient should receive rabies immunoglobulin and full rabies
vaccination schedule
The patient does not require rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
as he did not receive his injury in a high-risk region
The patient should receive rabies immunoglobulin but not rabies
vaccination as this is only of benefit if given pre-exposure

The patient was well in himself and denied any neurological or other
symptoms. He had no significant past medical history and took no
regular medications. He admitted that he had no adequately researched
his travel health needs before leaving the UK and so had not had any
vaccinations prior to his trip.
Examination of the patients wound demonstrated fully healed scars
consistent with a bite marks across the palm and dorsal surface of the
wrist. The limb had normal neurological and vascular examination and
the patient reported normal function of the hand.
What is the correct statement regarding rabies post-exposure

options: The patient should receive rabies vaccination but not rabies immunoglobulin as his wound has now healed
The patient does not require post-exposure prophylaxis as he remains free of symptoms following the incubation period of rabies
The patient should receive rabies immunoglobulin and full rabies vaccination schedule
The patient does not require rabies post-exposure prophylaxis as he did not receive his injury in a high-risk region
The patient should receive rabies immunoglobulin but not rabies vaccination as this is only of benefit if given pre-exposure
explanation:
The patient requires immediate (if belated) rabies post-exposure
prophylaxis. Penetrating wounds are considered high risk-exposures,
especially those to highly innervated areas such as the hands. The
history of an unprovoked animal biting is also of concern.
Rabies immunoglobulin should be given no matter how long has elapsed
since the exposure. As much as possible of the immunoglobulin dose
should be infiltrated around the wound, with the remainder given as an
IM gluteal injection. This should be combined with a full course of rabies
vaccination (typically a 5-dose schedule with doses at day 0, 3, 7, 14 and
28). Such post-exposure prophylaxis is highly effective in preventing the
rabies virus reaching the nervous system.
Large parts of South America and Central America (including Brazil) are
considered high-risk rabies regions. The virus is also endemic in Africa,
the Middle East, Eastern Europe and most of Asia.
The incubation period of rabies can be prolonged and the patient is
certainly still at risk of contracting the disease. One study found a mean
incubation time of 274 days (range 12 days to 10 years).
Crowcroft N, Thampi N. The prevention and management of rabies. BMJ
2015;350:g7827.

A 25-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a one-month history of
persistent, watery diarrhoea that is sometimes difficult to flush but never
bloody. She also reports associated bloating and flatulence. Since
returning from a trip to South America, she has experienced increasing
weakness and an inability to maintain her usual level of physical activity.
Over this period, she has lost 10 kg in weight but denies joint pains.
On examination, she is afebrile. Neurological examination shows no
abnormalities. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal first (S1) and second
(S2) heart sounds without additional sounds or murmurs. There are no
skin rashes present.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Amoebic dysentery
Coeliac disease
Giardiasis
Traveller's diarrhea

Question 151 of 287
A 25-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a one-month history of
persistent, watery diarrhoea that is sometimes difficult to flush but never
bloody. She also reports associated bloating and flatulence. Since
returning from a trip to South America, she has experienced increasing
weakness and an inability to maintain her usual level of physical activity.
Over this period, she has lost 10 kg in weight but denies joint pains.
On examination, she is afebrile. Neurological examination shows no
abnormalities. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal first (S1) and second
(S2) heart sounds without additional sounds or murmurs. There are no
skin rashes present.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Giardiasis is the correct answer.
Giardiasis should be considered in cases of persistent non-bloody
diarrhoea, mainly when it presents as watery and sometimes
steatorrhea. Accompanying symptoms may include lethargy, bloating,
Ongoing diarrhoea, lethargy, bloating, flatulence, steatorrhoea,
weight loss +/- recent travel → ?giardiasis
flatulence, and weight loss. G. lamblia transmission occurs via the fecal-
oral route, often through contaminated water or food. The parasite can
produce cysts resistant to chlorine and other disinfectants, complicating
its eradication from water supplies. Upon ingestion, the cysts excyst
within the small intestine and release trophozoites that adhere to the
intestinal wall and proliferate.
Amoebic dysentery is incorrect. E.histolytica, the cause of amoebic
dysentery, also follows a faecal-oral transmission route, usually via
contaminated food or water. Post-ingestion, this parasite may invade the
intestinal lining, causing abdominal discomfort and diarrhoea with
potentially bloody stools. Additionally, it can disseminate to other
organs, including the liver, lungs, and brain, leading to severe infections
which could be life-threatening. However, given the presence of
steatorrhea in this scenario, E.histolytica is less likely.
Coeliac disease is a long-term autoimmune disorder primarily affecting
the small intestine, where individuals develop intolerance to gluten,
which is present in foods such as wheat, rye and barley. Abnormal bowel
response to the ingested gluten leads to villous atrophy and subsequent
destruction of surface absorption observed in the duodenum and
jejunum. Although the symptoms are similar to giardiasis, the relation
between symptoms and travelling makes giardiasis more likely. Testing
for coeliac disease may be considered part of investigations if the
treatment for giardiasis is unsuccessful.
Traveller's diarrhoea is incorrect. Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC)
is the most common cause of traveller's diarrhoea and is typically
associated with watery diarrhoea that may occasionally contain blood
rather than steatorrhea. The presence of steatorrhea makes it unlikely.
Whipple's disease caused by T.whipplei,—is a rare condition
predominantly affecting middle-aged men and can manifest with
gastrointestinal symptoms, including steatorrhoea. Nevertheless, the
absence of additional signs like joint pain, central nervous system
involvement or headaches makes this diagnosis unlikely in this context.

A 45-year-old male from Afghanistan presents with a rash all over his
body. He describes the rash and suggests that it was initially multiple
specks of light skin that were not raised or roughened. they have now
progressed to plaques, some of which have become nodular.
He is otherwise well and his past medical history is significant only for
the successful treatment of visceral leishmaniasis in his home country
some 5 years ago.
What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a classic description of post kala azar dermal leishmaniasis
(PKDL) from an area where the disease is endemic. Leishmaniasis can
manifest as cutaneous, muco-cutaneous and visceral disease. PKDL is a
chronic skin condition that arises after the treatment of visceral disease.
The skin condition can arise months or years after successful treatment
and often presents with erythematous or hypo-pigmented macules that
may progress to become nodular. Clinically the lesions look very similar
to pityriasis versicolour, however this has a predilection for the chest and
back and is likely to have a scaly appearance rather than nodular.
Perhaps the most important differential is leprosy and lesions should be
tested for anaesthesia which would be strongly indicative for leprosy
over PKDL.
Although HIV can cause a myriad of skin pathology there is nothing
given in the question to make this a likely diagnosis and the best answer
is therefore PKDL.

explanation:
Trimethoprim is associated with a reversible elevation in serum
creatinine because of a reduction in tubular excretion. Creatinine returns
to normal once therapy ceases, and there is no effect on the GFR.
There is no suggestion of postural drop on blood pressure testing to
support either pre-renal failure or amlodipine being the likely cause of
creatinine elevation, and it's likely that the lisinopril has been prescribed
for a prolonged period, rather than it being the cause of an acute rise in
creatinine due to renal artery stenosis.
There are no symptoms of urinary obstruction to suggest post-renal
failure.

Diagnosis of TB fulfilling WHO clinical criteria
Initial response to anti-retroviral treatment

features of TB, CNS TB or TB serositis
Minor: New or worsening constitutional symptoms, respiratory
symptoms or abdominal pain.

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome

explanation:

be suspected in any patient with non-healing, scaling skin lesions,
particularly if they have been in an endemic area.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is typically diagnosed using a punch

Blood cultures is incorrect. Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease, blood

explanation:
The regular use of B-lactam antibiotics for urinary tract infection has
resulted in the emergence of new strains of bacteria that are resistant to
these antibiotics. ESBL is one of the most problematic strains that is
usually difficult to treat.
First line antibiotics are still carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem,
ertapenem, doripenem).
Giving these antibiotics may further increase resistance so the advice is
not to give antibiotics unless there are clinical signs and symptoms of a
urinary tract infection.

resistance and extended-spectrum beta-lactamases: Types,
epidemiology and treatment. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences, 22(1),
pp.90-101.

Her past medical history was unremarkable apart from being on the oral
contraceptive pill. She had been recovering from a widespread, pruritic,
vesicular rash over the past 8 days after coming into contact with her
nephew with chickenpox. Yesterday she began to feel lethargic and
unwell, with a high temperature and a painful left calf. This morning she
had noticed an area of erythema on her lower leg which seemed to get
larger and more painful throughout the day.
On examination, she looked unwell. There were healed varicella scars
and a few crusted scabs present over her lower limbs and torso. There
was a diffuse erythematous rash extending from her mid-calf to her
ankle. The area was oedematous and very tender. She had a normal
range of movement in all joints of the leg, albeit limited by pain.

What is the next most appropriate step in management?
options: Whilst IV aciclovir is important in the treatment of acute varicella IV aciclovir
Treatment dose low molecular weight heparin
explanation:
This is a case of bacterial superinfection complicating acute varicella
infection. The systemic involvement and rapid spread of cellulitis despite
broad-spectrum antibiotics should alert you to the possible diagnosis of
necrotising fasciitis. Whilst the most common type of necrotising
fasciitis is type 1 (caused by polymicrobial infection), most cases of
post-varicella necrotising fasciitis are caused by a monomicrobial
infection by group A streptococcus (e.g. Streptococcus pyogenes).
Bacteria are introduced into the skin via skin trauma (in this case, the
varicella skin lesions formed a portal of entry) and track along fascial
planes, extending beyond the area of overlying cellulitis.
The definite management of necrotising fasciitis is surgical debridement
of all infected tissue. As the infection progresses, necrosis and
hypoperfusion of the area limit the delivery of antibiotics to the area.
Without debridement, mortality is 100% and any delay increases the risk
of death.
Chickenpox is a risk factor for invasive group A streptococcal soft
tissue infections including necrotizing fasciitis
infection, the most important next step is to remove the source of the
bacterial infection. Chickenpox has contributed to this presentation but
is not the cause of her acute deterioration or necrotic skin.
Whilst MRI can confirm the extent of necrotising fasciitis, it may delay
surgical debridement. This patient is clearly unwell and needs immediate
definitive management.
Treatment dose low molecular weight heparin would be appropriate if
the cause was a deep vein thrombosis but this presentation is more in
keeping with a rapidly progressive bacterial infection.
Plasmapheresis does not have a role in the management of necrotising
fasciitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a viral haemorrhagic fever, and the clinical picture is classic for
dengue. The disease is endemic in South-East Asia. A defective immune
response in secondary infections means that individuals who have been
infected with one viral serotype may develop more severe disease when
later infected with a different serotype. This patient may have developed
self-limiting dengue fever on a previous trip to Vietnam, and now has
secondary infection.
Retro-orbital headache, fever, facial flushing, rash,
thrombocytopenia in returning traveller → ?dengue
Dengue fever typically begins 7-10 days after infection with a rapid onset
of fever, severe myalgia, and retro-orbital headache. A maculopapular
rash with islands of sparing is characteristic. In the majority of cases
there is self-resolution after 2-7 days. In a proportion of cases however,
especially in secondary infection, the disease progresses to a more
fulminant form known as dengue haemorrhagic fever. There is
widespread vascular breakdown, with easy bleeding and bruising.
Thrombocytopaenia is typical. Plasma leakage results in
haemoconcentration, raising the haemocrit, and loss of plasma proteins
into the extracellular space is reflected by the low albumin. The liver is
often enlarged and tender, with deranged liver function tests. In severe
cases this progresses to circulatory collapse and dengue shock
syndrome. Diagnosis is by PCR (polymerase chain reaction) during the
initial febrile phase and serology during the later stages. Management is
supportive.
Non-falciparum malaria includes disease caused by Plasmodium vivax
and ovale, and to a lesser extent malariae and knowlesi. Vivax is common
in Thailand and typically causes less severe disease. Most malaria rapid
diagnostic tests are antigen assays that detect only falciparum.
Microscopy is the only way to confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic fever endemic to West Africa.
Meningococcal septicaemia is a possibility, although one would expect
him to be more unwell after five days of disease.
HIV seroconversion illness does not commonly cause bleeding
manifestations.
Dengue fever

mother who lived in the same house as him was diagnosed with

Examination of his cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and
neurological systems were all entirely unremarkable.
Initial investigations revealed the following:
Blood film:negative; including negative malaria screen
Blood culture: negative culture; awaiting prolonged acid-fast bacilli
culture result
Quantaferon blood test: positive
Mantoux test: positive
Chest x-ray: normal appearances of heart and lung fields, no abnormality
was seen
Based upon the above information, what is the next best management
step?
options: Tuberculosis: latent disease Commence treatment with isoniazid, pyridoxine, ethambutol, rifampicin and pyrazinamide for 2 months
Discharge from clinic with no further action to take
Refer for diagnostic bronchoscopy alveolar lavage
Commence isoniazid and pyridoxine for 6 months
Repeat Quantaferon blood test weekly for the next month - treat if remains positive
explanation:
This gentleman has latent TB. He has had close (and presumably
prolonged) contact with an active TB carrier but other than the presence
of transient symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection has been
asymptomatic. He has had a positive Mantoux test, which can be
positive with both active and latent TB but can also by a previous BCG
vaccination. Quantiferon testing, on the other hand, is not influenced by
BCG vaccination status but cannot distinguish between active and latent
TB. However in the absence of significant symptoms and with normal
investigations including a normal CXR the most likely diagnosis is latent
TB and therefore he requires monotherapy with isoniazid (and
pyridoxine) for 6 months.
Latent tuberculosis treatment options:
3 months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin, or
6 months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine)

explanation:
The prodromal phase of malaise and possible personality change,
followed by meningism, with the onset of basal cranial nerve palsies, and
coupled with the CSF findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein,
and low glucose, are all highly suggestive of tuberculous meningitis.
There is no particular suggestion of a primary malignancy, but malignant
meningitis (leptomeningeal carcinomatosis) is a possibility and it would
be reasonable to send a large volume of CSF for cytology. Like
tuberculous meningitis, this condition typically presents with headache,
meningism, and cranial nerve palsies. However, it is eye movements
which are most often affected. There is often also invasion of spinal
meninges which involves nerve roots and mimics radiculopathy. The CSF
is hardly ever normal, although there are no specific features other than
the direct demonstration of malignant cells.
Meningococcal meningitis is an acute disease, so the three week
prodrome described here would be unusual. The presence of cranial
nerve palsies would be extremely unusual. The CSF would be expected
to show a neutrophilic pleocytosis, with a low glucose (less that 50% of
serum glucose), but not as low as in tuberculous meningitis.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage should be considered in any case of acute
headache. The normal CT scan is reassuring but does not exclude the
diagnosis, but in any case the CSF is not suggestive.
A tumour of the skull base might explain the lower cranial nerve palsies,
but one would have expected some more suggestive symptoms and an
abnormal CT head. This diagnosis would not explain the grossly
abnormal CSF findings.

with hepatitis C. A test for HIV viral tropism is reported as dual tropism

Maraviroc
Raltegravir
Tenofovir
Ribavirin

Question 168 of 287
A 54-year-old intravenous drug user is newly diagnosed with HIV, after
presenting with progressive shortness of breath. He was diagnosed with
pneumocystis pneumonia and commenced on appropriate treatment.
His CD4 count is 54 cells/mm3 and his viral load is 1.7 x10^7 copies per
ml.
As part of his routine workup, it is also revealed that he has co-infection
with hepatitis C. A test for HIV viral tropism is reported as dual tropism
virus.
Which drug is unlikely to be effective in this man's treatment?
explanation:
HIV binds to the CD4 cell via the CD4 receptor. This interaction also
depends on viral interaction with the CD4 co-receptor. There are two
forms of CD4 co-receptor CCR5 and CXCR4.
The test for viral tropism determines which of these co-receptors HIV
will bind to. Maraviroc blocks HIV binding to the CCR5 receptor, and
therefore is an effective drug in a 'CCR5 tropic' virus. However, it is not
effective if the virus is 'CXCR4 tropic' or 'dual tropic'. The tropism of HIV
will not affect the use of any of the other drugs listed.
It is routine to test HIV viral tropism on diagnosis, or on virological failure
to assess if maraviroc is a therapeutic option.

explanation:
Interactions between anti-reteroviral drugs and other more common
medications are many and varied. It is a complex area but is one that is
becoming more prominent given the larger prevalance of HIV. HIV is no
longer a death sentence and with current treatments patients can expect
to have an almost normal life expectancy. Full knowledge of all the
possible interactions is unrealistic but some of the main ones should be
kept in mind when prescribing any new medication. There is an excellent
resource kept by the University of Liverpool that can be found at
In the case detailed above the patient is likely to have been started on a
PPI such as Lansoprazole. Lansoprazole is known to dangerously lower
the efficacy of atazanavir and this is exhibited by the dramatic fall in CD4
count. This patient also seems to have developed oesophageal
candidiasis and so urgent management to manage his HIV is required to
avoid potentially deadly opportunistic infections.

explanation:
This patient is systemically unwell with a rapidly progressive soft tissue
infection. Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for necrotising fasciitis and
his recent operation served as a cutaneous portal of entry for causative
organisms. A rapidly expanding area of cellulitis in a systemically unwell
patient should alert you to the possible diagnosis of necrotising fasciitis.
Furthermore, the presence of anaesthesia of the area and pain out of
keeping with the visible skin changes is also characteristic of this
condition. Whilst necrotising fasciitis is often seen in the extremities, it
can also occur in the perineum, head, neck, and trunk.
The most common cause of necrotising fasciitis is type 1, caused by
polymicrobial infection of subcutaneous tissue (organisms present
include Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, E. coli, Enterobacter, etc).
Bacteria are introduced into the skin via minor skin trauma or surgery
and track along fascial planes, extending beyond the area of overlying
cellulitis.
Type 2 necrotising fasciitis is a monomicrobial infection most commonly
caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.
Aeromonas hydrophila is a less common cause of necrotising fasciitis,
typically associated with freshwater exposure.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is a commensal organism present on the
skin and the most common cause of infections from indwelling medical
devices.

Bacillus anthracis, a gram-positive bacteria, causes cutaneous anthrax.

Necrotising fasciitis is a medical emergency that is difficult to recognise

Question 171 of 287
A 32-year-old gentleman presents to the emergency department with
severe nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. He was recently at a reunion
where 18 out of 25 guests have developed similar symptoms shortly
afterwards. On examination he appears clinically dehydrated but his vital
parameters are all normal. He has no past medical history and otherwise
his examination is normal. You suspect norovirus; what is the most
appropriate investigation?
explanation:
The correct answer is faecal or vomitus viral PCR which can confirm
norovirus infection. Tests can detect antibodies by the ELISA method but
these lack sensitivity and specificity and are therefore seldom used in
the clinical setting. Norovirus does not make a toxin and therefore there
is no such thing as norovirus toxin testing. The virus is not normally
present in the bloodstream and therefore serum is likely to be negative
for PCR testing. Norovirus is a viral cause of gastroenteritis commonly
associated with large outbreaks in winter.

explanation:
A number of features suggest neurosyphilis from the history. Firstly, the
likely aortic regurgitation on cardiovascular examination should make
you suspicious of aortitis, of which syphilitic infection is a classic cause.
He has had a range of sexually transmitted diseases. A painless red rash
is also a classic sign of syphilis, particularly in palms of the hands or the
soles of the feet. He also has a combined upgoing plantar with absent
ankle jerks, which narrows the diagnosis to the classic five MRCP
favourite of motor neurone disease, tabes dorsalis, subacute combined
degeneration of the cord, Friedrich's ataxia and dual pathology of central
and peripheral causes. There is little to suggest a genetic disorder
presenting in his mid-40s or a vitamin B deficiency to account for SCDC.
Neurosyphilis would be the most likely diagnosis.

Chikungunya can present with debilitating joint pain. A rash develops in
up to 75% of patients. The most common symptoms include fevers and
malaise. It can be difficult to differentiate from dengue early in the
disease. Two significant differences may help distinguish between them;
1) In chikungunya, rashes appear on the torso and the arms while in
dengue, they appear on the arms and the face. 2) Joint pain in
chikungunya is experienced in the hands, wrists, feet, and legs, while in
dengue it is experienced in the shoulders and the knees.
Dengue is an important differential diagnosis. It is a mosquito-borne
tropical disease caused by the dengue virus. Symptoms include a high
fever, headache, vomiting, joint pains, and a characteristic skin rash. It
may be indistinguishable from chikungunya early in the disease.
Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric polyarthritis involving large and
small joints. This is unlikely given the acute presentation, and
rheumatoid arthritis is not typically associated with fevers or rash.
Malaria should be considered in any patient with fevers and non-specific
symptoms travelling from an endemic area. It may present with fevers,
malaise, diaphoresis, headaches, cough, arthralgia. Chikungunya is more
likely in our patient as it more commonly presents with joint pains and
rash.
Chikungunya can present with debilitating joint pain
characteristic scaly rash. The acute presentation and fevers suggest an
infectious cause.

presentation of high fever with right upper abdominal pain and
tenderness soon after returning from an endemic area (Central America)
should raise suspicion of an amoebic liver abscess caused by
Entamoeba histolytica infection. This is supported by leucocytosis and
elevated liver enzymes. Although his bowel habits are normal, amoebic
liver abscess frequently occurs without diarrhoea. Treatment would
typically involve a course of metronidazole followed by a luminal agent
such as diloxanide.
Hepatocellular adenoma is an unlikely diagnosis in this case. These
benign liver tumours typically remain asymptomatic and do not cause
the acute symptoms presented by this patient. The high fever and right
upper quadrant pain are inconsistent with the usual presentation of
hepatocellular adenoma. Additionally, the patient's laboratory results,
particularly the elevated white blood cell count and liver enzymes, are
not typical features of this condition.
Hepatocellular carcinoma is improbable in this scenario. While it can
cause right upper quadrant pain, it usually develops in older individuals
or those with underlying liver disease. The acute onset of symptoms,
high fever, and the patient's young age (32 years) make this diagnosis
unlikely. Furthermore, hepatocellular carcinoma typically presents with
more gradual changes in liver function tests and often with signs of
chronic liver disease, which are not evident in this case.
Hydatid cyst, caused by Echinococcus granulosus infection, although a
consideration in travellers, is less likely in this scenario. Hydatid cysts
usually grow slowly and remain asymptomatic for years. The acute
presentation with high fever (39.8°C) and severe right upper quadrant
pain is atypical for a hydatid cyst. Moreover, hydatid cysts rarely cause
such significant elevations in white blood cell count or liver enzymes as
seen in this patient.
Pyogenic liver abscess is less likely due to the patient's young age, lack
of comorbidities, and recent travel to Central America, favouring an
amoebic liver abscess. Pyogenic abscesses often have a more subacute
course, are associated with jaundice or sepsis, and typically occur in
older or immunocompromised patients. The acute presentation,
moderate leukocytosis, mildly elevated liver enzymes, and normal
albumin further support an amoebic rather than pyogenic origin.

The Medical Emergency Team (MET) is summoned to the Surgical Unit
to assist with the management of an acutely unwell patient.
The patient is a 21-year-old male who underwent open surgery for
perforated appendicitis 3 days ago. The Surgical Registrar informs you
that faecal contamination of the abdomen was noted during the
operation and that a peritoneal washout was performed.
24 hours later, the patient began to complain of worsening abdominal
pain. He became febrile in the early hours of the morning and blood
cultures were taken. Since then, he has become progressively more
unwell. He was taken down for an urgent abdominal ultrasound mid-
afternoon, but the nurses were so concerned about his condition when
he arrived back on the ward that a MET call was put out.
On examination, the patient is responsive to voice. He is febrile at
38.9ºC, his pulse is 131bpm and his blood pressure is 72/53mmHg. His
peripheries are warm and clammy. Palpation of the abdomen reveals
localised tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa. The surgical
wound appears clean with minimal surrounding erythema.
As you prepare to place a large bore IV cannula the Surgical FY1 passes
you some results that have recently been phoned through:
Abdominal ultrasound
Anechoic fluid collection in the right iliac fossa
Blood culture
Gram-positive cocci both bottles - further information to follow

Anechoic fluid collection in the right iliac fossa
Blood culture

Which of the following organisms is most likely to be isolated from the
blood culture?
explanation:
Although on first glance this may appear to be a 'surgical case', it is
important to remember that MET or 'crash' teams are called to attend a
variety of patients, some of whom may be admitted under the care of
other specialties. On-call medical doctors need to be able to apply their
knowledge to a range of situations, particularly when they fall outwith
the remit of their day-to-day practice.
A significant amount of surgical information is presented in this vignette,
however, the underlying diagnosis is given to the candidate and the
question is actually designed to test the candidate's knowledge of
pathogenic bacteria and the illnesses they cause.
Strep. pyogenes is a common cause of pharyngitis and soft tissue
infections, occasionally giving rise to septicaemia. It would be unlikely to
cause illness in the case described above.
Staph. aureus and Staph. epidermidis are commensal organisms that
commonly cause septicaemia in critically ill patients, often secondary to
the colonisation of indwelling lines. This vignette makes no mention of
any such devices and we are told that the surgical wound is clean,
making primary staphylococcal wound infection unlikely.
Escherichia coli is a gram-negative bacillus and is, therefore,
inconsistent with the blood culture results described.
Enterococcus faecalis is a group D streptococcus. It is a gut commensal
and a well-known cause of intra-abdominal infections. In the case
described, it is likely that faecal contamination of the abdomen lead to
the formation of an abscess and consequent Enterococcus
bacteraemia.

has no past medical history and is not on any regular medications. He
has recently returned from spending six months in Equatorial Guinea.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Loiasis is the correct answer. The patient presents with transient, non-
erythematous, hot swellings of the soft tissues around joints. This is a
description of so-called Calabar swellings, which are associated with
loiasis. This condition is a filarial infection caused by the nematode Loa
Loa. The Calabar swellings are caused by an immune reaction to the
worms. Eosinophilia is common in this condition and it is endemic to
Equatorial Guinea.
Cutaneous larva migrans is incorrect. This can cause skin lesions and
eosinophilia. However, the lesions in this condition (which is caused by a
hookworm infection) are classically serpiginous in outline and therefore
a 2x3cm lesion would not be characteristic.
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is incorrect. This condition is transmitted by
sandflies. It characteristically causes an ulcerative lesion, which is not
present in this case as there is no mention of skin erosion. Additionally,
the lesions tend not to be transient and persist without treatment.
Schistosomiasis is incorrect. An acute schistosomiasis infection is
typically characterized by fever, blotchy rash, myalgia, arthralgia and
diarrhoea. So while it is endemic in Equatorial Guinea and associated
with blood eosinophilia, the presentation is not characteristic of the
disease.
Syphilis is incorrect. This can cause a skin lesion called a chancre, which
is a painless ulcer. However, this typically occurs on the genitals and
occurs once rather than episodically. Additionally, eosinophilia is not
typical of this condition.

A 35-year-old woman presents to the ambulatory medical care unit with
a 6-week history of an ulcer on the back of her right hand. It started as a
1cm painful nodule and gradually enlarged. It is now 3cm in diameter
and is a firm raised purple/red lesion with some central ulceration. There
are no lesions anywhere else and she is systemically well. She has no
known past medical history and has not travelled outside of the UK in the
last 5 years. She has no pets but works in a pet shop which specialises
in tropical fish.
What organism is the most likely cause of this lesion?
Herpes simplex virus
Leishmania braziliensis
Mycobacterium marinum
Mycobacterium ulcerans
Sporothrix schenckii
Question 183 of 287
A 35-year-old woman presents to the ambulatory medical care unit with
a 6-week history of an ulcer on the back of her right hand. It started as a
1cm painful nodule and gradually enlarged. It is now 3cm in diameter
and is a firm raised purple/red lesion with some central ulceration. There
are no lesions anywhere else and she is systemically well. She has no
known past medical history and has not travelled outside of the UK in the
last 5 years. She has no pets but works in a pet shop which specialises
in tropical fish.
What organism is the most likely cause of this lesion?
explanation:
This presentation is typical of fish tank granuloma, which is caused by
Mycobacterium marinum. The main clue is her exposure to fish tanks and
lack of risk factors for the other organisms. As well as via contact of
skin with the water in fish tanks or aquariums, the infection can less
commonly be acquired through preparing fish or shellfish, or contact
with fishing equipment. It generally presents as a slow-growing lesion,
although it may disseminate or progress more quickly in immune-
suppressed people. Mycobacterium marinum grows most effectively at
30 degrees, and so the lesions are usually found at the extremities.
Fish tank granuloma is caused by Mycobacterium marinum
Herpes simplex virus can cause lesions on the hand if the skin of the
hand comes into contact with infected skin around the mouth or genitals
- this is called herpetic whitlow. However, the lesion would usually be on
the fingertips rather than the back of the hand, would start with vesicles
rather than a nodule, and would generally progress more quickly.
Leishmania braziliensis causes cutaneous and mucocutaneous
leishmaniasis and is found in Central and South America. Cutaneous
leishmaniasis may present similarly to fish tank granuloma, however, the
patient has not travelled abroad.
Mycobacterium ulcerans causes painful ulcers on the skin which are
often called Buruli ulcers - however, it is found predominantly in tropical
regions.

explanation:
The diagnosis is cryptosporidium infection. It is the most common

visualisation with modified Zeihl-Neelson stain of stool. You would very
rarely expect to see Mycobacterium tuberculosis on a faecal sample.
